title: DATA SELECTION AND FILTERING
introRaw:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
Most analysis starts with choosing WHICH rows and columns to look at. Every
selection defines a SUBSET of the data; every statistic you compute
afterwards describes THAT subset, not necessarily the population you
began with. Filtering is therefore a statistical decision, not just a
technical step.

sections.title: DATA SUBSETS

blocks.rawText:
SELECTING COLUMNS: df["age"] (Series), df[["age", "city"]] (DataFrame),
   df.select_dtypes("number"), df.filter(like="inc"), df.drop(columns=["id"]).
SELECTING ROWS BY POSITION OR LABEL: df.iloc[0:3] (first three rows),
   df.loc[0:3] (labels 0-3 inclusive), df.head(n), df.tail(n),
   df.sample(n=100, random_state=0) (random subset), df.nlargest(3, "income"),
   df.sort_values("age").iloc[:5].
SELECTING BY CONDITION: boolean indexing (42.2).
SUBSET FOR A PURPOSE: train/validation/test splits (Module 46), stratified
subsamples, time-based windows (df[df.date >= "2024-01-01"]), one
customer segment.
INDEX AFTER SUBSETTING: labels are preserved (rows 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 after
filtering); use .reset_index(drop=True) if positional numbering is
needed, and .copy() if you will modify the subset.

sections.title: BOOLEAN INDEXING

blocks.rawText:
IDEA: a condition on a column produces a BOOLEAN MASK (one True/False per row);
using it as an index keeps the rows where the mask is True.
   m = df["age"] > 30
   m.tolist() -> [False, True, True, True, True, False, False, True]
   m.sum() -> 5 (number of rows satisfying the condition)
   m.mean() -> proportion of rows satisfying the condition (5/8 = 0.625,
      counting the NaN row as False)
   df[m]        # rows 2, 3, 4, 5, 8 (ids); the row with age NaN is excluded
   df.loc[m, ["id", "city"]]    # rows AND columns in one step
USEFUL BOOLEAN TOOLS
   df["city"].isin(["Pune", "Delhi"])         # membership -> ids 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8
   df["age"].between(30, 50)                   # INCLUSIVE both ends -> ids 2, 3, 5
   df["age"].isna() / .notna()                 # missing / present
   df["city"].str.contains("pu", case=False)   # text patterns (regex allowed)
   df.query("age > 30 and city == 'Delhi'")    # readable string syntax -> ids 2, 5, 8
   (query accepts and/or/not; use @var to refer to Python variables.)
   df.duplicated(subset=["id"])                # duplicate rows
FILTERING THE POPULATION OF A STATISTIC: df.loc[df.city == "Pune", "churn"].mean()
   -> 0.0 (churn rate among Pune customers); df.loc[df.income > 50, "churn"]
   .mean() -> 0.5. These ARE conditional probabilities/means, P(churn | Pune)
   and P(churn | income > 50): the filter is the conditioning event
   (Module 34).

sections.title: FILTERING WITH MULTIPLE CONDITIONS: LOGICAL AND/OR

blocks.rawText:
AND (&): rows satisfying BOTH conditions: the INTERSECTION; narrows.
   OR  (|): rows satisfying AT LEAST ONE condition: the UNION; widens.
   NOT (~): rows NOT satisfying the condition: the COMPLEMENT.
   Always bracket each comparison.
VERIFIED RESULTS on the example DataFrame
   (df.age > 30) & (df.city == "Pune")   -> id 3 only (a single row)
   (df.age > 30) | (df.city == "Pune")   -> ids 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8
   ~(df.age > 30)                         -> ids 1, 6, 7 (!)
   df[df.age <= 30]                        -> ids 1, 6
   df[df.age > 30]                         -> ids 2, 3, 4, 5, 8
   TRAP: id 7 (age NaN) appears in ~(age > 30) but in NEITHER age <= 30
   NOR age > 30. Decide explicitly what to do with missing values:
   (df.age <= 30) | df.age.isna().
COUNTING (inclusion-exclusion, Module 33): if 40 rows satisfy A, 30 satisfy
   B and 12 satisfy both, then |A OR B| = 40 + 30 - 12 = 58 and
   |A AND NOT B| = 28. In code: (A | B).sum() equals A.sum() + B.sum() -
   (A & B).sum().
DE MORGAN (Module 23): ~((df.age > 30) & (df.city == "Pune")) equals
   (df.age <= 30) | (df.city != "Pune") when no values are missing.
ERRORS TO AVOID
   - Using and/or/not with Series: ValueError "The truth value of a Series is
     ambiguous".
   - Missing brackets: df.age > 30 & df.city == "Pune" is parsed as
     df.age > (30 & df.city) == "Pune": an error or nonsense.
   - Chained filters on a copy followed by assignment (SettingWithCopy);
     use df.loc[mask, "col"] = value.
   - Silent row loss: ALWAYS print row counts before and after filtering,
     and use assert statements for expectations (assert len(df2) > 0).

sections.title: DATAFRAME OPERATIONS FOR SELECTION AND SUMMARIZING

blocks.rawText:
Create/transform columns  df.assign(income_k=lambda d: d.income / 1000)
   Conditional column         np.where(df.income > 50, "high", "low")
   Binning                    pd.cut(df.age, [0, 30, 50, 100]); pd.qcut(df.income, 4)
   Group summaries            df.groupby("city")["churn"].mean()
   Counts and proportions     df["city"].value_counts(normalize=True)
   Combine tables             pd.merge(left, right, on="id", how="left")
   Reshape                    df.pivot_table(...), df.melt(...)
   Sort, rank, top-k          df.sort_values("income").head(3), df.nlargest(3, "income")
   Remove duplicates          df.drop_duplicates(subset="id", keep="first")
   Apply a function           df["age"].map(f), df.apply(f, axis=1) (slow)
   Method chaining (readable pipelines):
      (df.query("age > 30")
         .assign(income_k=lambda d: d.income / 1000)
         .groupby("city")["income_k"].mean())

sections.title: UNDERSTANDING THE POPULATION REPRESENTED BY A FILTERED DATASET

blocks.rawText:
PRINCIPLE: a filtered dataset represents the SUBPOPULATION satisfying the
filter (and any earlier selection steps). Statistics computed on it are
estimates for THAT subpopulation, and may be misleading for the original one.
Ask: "Which population does the remaining data represent, and is that
the population I want conclusions about?"
KEY CONSEQUENCES
   1. CONDITIONAL, NOT MARGINAL: the churn rate among Pune customers is
      P(churn | Pune), not P(churn). Report which subset a number refers
      to.
   2. SELECTION (SURVIVORSHIP) BIAS: analyzing only customers who completed
      a purchase, only companies that still exist, or only patients who
      returned for follow-up gives a biased picture of everyone.
   3. COMPLETE-CASE ANALYSIS changes the population unless data are
      missing completely at random. Example (verified): incomes 20, 25, 30,
      35, 40, 200, 250, 300 have mean 112.5, but dropping rows where the
      three largest are unreported leaves mean 30.0 (5 rows): the filter
      (dropna) removed the high earners.
   4. RANGE RESTRICTION LOWERS CORRELATION: for x = 1..10 and y = 2, 1, 4, 3, 6,
      5, 8, 7, 10, 9 the correlation is 0.939; filtering to x >= 6 gives 0.822.
      A model fitted on a narrow slice may show weaker relationships (and
      predict poorly outside the slice).
   5. OUTLIER REMOVAL shrinks variance and changes the mean, and defines the
      population as "non-extreme cases". Document and justify.
   6. COLLIDER/BERKSON EFFECTS: selecting on a variable influenced by both
      X and Y (e.g. only hospital patients, only admitted students) can
      create associations that do not exist in the full population.
   7. TRAIN/DEPLOYMENT MISMATCH: a model trained on a filtered subset is
      valid only for similar cases; test data must reflect the population
      where the model will be used (Module 46). Filtering rows by the
      TARGET (keeping only converted leads) leaks information and creates
      a biased training set.
   8. WEIGHTS: if a subset over- or under-represents groups, use sampling
      weights or stratified analysis to recover population estimates
      (Module 26 weighted means).
   9. SIMPSON'S PARADOX: overall trends can reverse within filtered
      subgroups, so subgroup filters can change conclusions (Module 40.8).
CHECKLIST: record every filter in order, row counts at each step, how
missing values were treated, and the population the final dataset represents;
compare summary statistics of the subset with the full data to see how
it differs.

sections.title: DATA CLEANING AND PREPROCESSING

blocks.rawText:
TYPICAL PIPELINE (in this order of thinking)
   1. INSPECT: df.info(), df.describe(include="all"), df.isna().sum(),
      value_counts for categoricals, plot distributions.
   2. FIX TYPES: numbers stored as text (pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce")),
      dates (pd.to_datetime), categories (astype("category")).
   3. DUPLICATES AND KEYS: df.duplicated().sum(); check that key columns
      are unique when they should be.
   4. TEXT STANDARDIZATION: .str.strip(), .str.lower(), unify spellings
      ("N. Delhi" vs "New Delhi"), units (cm vs m), currencies, time zones.
   5. MISSING VALUES: investigate the mechanism (MCAR/MAR/MNAR); drop,
      impute (median for skewed numeric: with age missing, the median of
      the 7 observed ages is 38.0, so age_f = df.age.fillna(38.0)),
      most frequent for categoricals, add a "was_missing" indicator.
   6. OUTLIERS AND IMPOSSIBLE VALUES: validate (negative ages, impossible
      dates); Tukey fences (Module 30) or domain limits; keep genuine
      extremes; winsorize if appropriate.
   7. ENCODE CATEGORICALS: one-hot (pd.get_dummies(df.city, drop_first=True)
      gives columns Mumbai, Pune with Delhi as the reference category,
      avoiding the dummy-variable trap), ordinal codes for ordered
      categories, target/frequency encoding with care (leakage).
   8. TRANSFORM AND SCALE (below).
   9. SPLIT AND PIPELINE: split into train/test BEFORE fitting imputers,
      scalers, encoders (fit on train, apply to test), preferably inside a
      scikit-learn Pipeline/ColumnTransformer so cross-validation does not
      leak (Module 46).
   10. VALIDATE: assertions for ranges, uniqueness, non-null columns;
       record data version and random seeds.

blocks.title: FEATURE SCALING FORMULAS
blocks.formulaBody:
Standardization (z-score):  z = (x - mean)/sd
     Min-max scaling to [0, 1]:  x' = (x - min)/(max - min)
     Robust scaling:             x' = (x - median)/IQR

parts.A: NAME: Standardization, min-max scaling, robust scaling.
parts.B:
FORMULAS
     Standardization (z-score):  z = (x - mean)/sd
     Min-max scaling to [0, 1]:  x' = (x - min)/(max - min)
     Robust scaling:             x' = (x - median)/IQR
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: mean, sd, min, max, median, IQR computed on the TRAINING data;
   IQR = Q3 - Q1.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: put features on comparable scales so that distance-based
   methods (k-NN, k-means, SVM, RBF kernels), gradient-based optimization,
   PCA and penalized regression are not dominated by the feature with the
   largest units. Tree-based models do not need scaling.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: choose by distribution: standardization for roughly
   symmetric data; min-max is sensitive to outliers (a single extreme value
   squeezes everything else); robust scaling tolerates outliers. Apply the
   SAME training-set constants to new data. Do not scale the target for
   trees unnecessarily; remember to invert transformations of y when
   reporting.
   !! DENOMINATOR CONVENTION !! sklearn StandardScaler divides by the
   POPULATION sd (ddof = 0); pandas .std() uses ddof = 1.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: values 10, 20, 30, 40, 100: mean 40, deviations -30, -20, -10, 0,
   60; sum of squares 5000.
   population sd = sqrt(5000/5) = 31.62 (sklearn): z = -0.949, -0.632,
      -0.316, 0, 1.897.
   sample sd = sqrt(5000/4) = 35.36 (pandas): z = -0.849, -0.566, -0.283, 0,
      1.697.
   min-max: (10, 20, 30, 40, 100) -> 0, 0.111, 0.222, 0.333, 1.
   robust: median 30, Q1 = 20, Q3 = 40, IQR = 20: -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 3.5.
   Note how the outlier 100 compresses the min-max values of the others
   into [0, 0.33], while robust scaling keeps them well spread.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: z = 1.9 means 1.9 sd above the mean; after standardizing,
   every feature has mean 0 and (population) sd 1; coefficients of a
   linear model on standardized features are comparable.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: computing the scaler on the whole dataset before splitting
   (leakage); scaling dummy variables unnecessarily; forgetting to apply
   the saved transformation at prediction time; using min-max with
   unbounded outliers.
parts.J:
RELATED: z-scores (Module 35), PCA (Module 10; needs centered/scaled
   data), regularization (Module 47).
LOG AND POWER TRANSFORMS: for right-skewed positive data use log(x) or
log1p(x) (handles zeros), square root, or Box-Cox/Yeo-Johnson; makes
multiplicative effects additive and often stabilizes variance (Module
40.7).

choices change the population (42.5).

   SAME training-set constants to new data. Do not scale the target for
   trees unnecessarily; remember to invert transformations of y when
   reporting.
   !! DENOMINATOR CONVENTION !! sklearn StandardScaler divides by the
   POPULATION sd (ddof = 0); pandas .std() uses ddof = 1.
G. EXAMPLE: values 10, 20, 30, 40, 100: mean 40, deviations -30, -20, -10, 0,
   60; sum of squares 5000.
   population sd = sqrt(5000/5) = 31.62 (sklearn): z = -0.949, -0.632,
      -0.316, 0, 1.897.
   sample sd = sqrt(5000/4) = 35.36 (pandas): z = -0.849, -0.566, -0.283, 0,
      1.697.
   min-max: (10, 20, 30, 40, 100) -> 0, 0.111, 0.222, 0.333, 1.
   robust: median 30, Q1 = 20, Q3 = 40, IQR = 20: -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 3.5.
   Note how the outlier 100 compresses the min-max values of the others
   into [0, 0.33], while robust scaling keeps them well spread.
H. INTERPRETATION: z = 1.9 means 1.9 sd above the mean; after standardizing,
   every feature has mean 0 and (population) sd 1; coefficients of a
   linear model on standardized features are comparable.
I. MISTAKES: computing the scaler on the whole dataset before splitting
   (leakage); scaling dummy variables unnecessarily; forgetting to apply
   the saved transformation at prediction time; using min-max with
   unbounded outliers.
J. RELATED: z-scores (Module 35), PCA (Module 10; needs centered/scaled
   data), regularization (Module 47).
LOG AND POWER TRANSFORMS: for right-skewed positive data use log(x) or
log1p(x) (handles zeros), square root, or Box-Cox/Yeo-Johnson; makes
multiplicative effects additive and often stabilizes variance (Module
40.7).
COMMON MISTAKES IN CLEANING: deleting rows without recording why; imputing
before splitting; treating -999 or 0 as real values (sentinel codes for
missing); changing categories inconsistently between train and test;
dropping outliers because they hurt a model's fit; ignoring that cleaning
choices change the population (42.5).

title: OPTIMIZATION ALGORITHMS
introRaw:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
Training almost every machine-learning model means finding parameters that
make a score as good as possible: the smallest error, the largest
likelihood. Optimization is the mathematics of "find the input that
makes this function as small (or large) as possible". Often no formula
gives the answer, so we search step by step, using the slope of the
function (derivatives, Modules 3 and 12) to decide which way to move.

sections.title: OBJECTIVE FUNCTIONS; MINIMIZATION AND MAXIMIZATION; CONVEXITY

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITIONS
   OBJECTIVE FUNCTION f(theta): the quantity to optimize, a function of the
      decision variables/parameters theta (a vector). Also called loss,
      cost, error (to minimize) or reward, likelihood, score (to maximize).
   MINIMIZATION PROBLEM:  minimize f(theta) over theta (optionally subject to
      constraints g(theta) <= 0, h(theta) = 0).
   argmin: the theta at which the minimum is attained; min is the value.
   MAXIMIZATION = MINIMIZATION of -f:  max f(theta) = - min (-f(theta));
      the maximizer is the same. (MLE: maximize log-likelihood = minimize
      negative log-likelihood, Module 38.)
EXAMPLES OF OBJECTIVES
   Mean squared error  (1/n) sum (y_i - x_i^T beta)^2   (regression)
   Cross-entropy       -(1/n) sum [y_i ln p_i + (1 - y_i) ln(1 - p_i)]
   Regularized loss    loss(theta) + lambda |theta|^2   (ridge)
   Negative log-likelihood; hinge loss (SVM); distance to centroids (k-means).

blocks.title: CONVEX FUNCTIONS
blocks.formulaBody:
f is CONVEX if for all x, y and every t in [0, 1]:
        f( t x + (1 - t) y ) <= t f(x) + (1 - t) f(y)
   (the chord between two points lies on or above the graph).
   For twice-differentiable f: convex <=> Hessian H(x) is positive
   semi-definite for all x (F9.5, F12.6). STRICTLY convex (H positive
   definite) => at most one minimizer.

parts.B:

   definite) => at most one minimizer.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: t the mixing weight between the two points.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: a convex function is bowl-shaped with no separate dips. KEY
   CONSEQUENCE: for a convex function every LOCAL minimum is a GLOBAL
   minimum, and gradient-based methods that converge find it.
parts.E:
EXAMPLES: convex: x^2, e^x, |x|, x ln x, MSE for linear models (Hessian
   (2/n) X^T X is PSD), logistic loss, hinge loss, ridge objective.
   NON-convex: x^4 - 3x^2 + x, neural-network losses, k-means objective,
   mixture-model likelihoods.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: f(x) = x^2: chord test with x = 0, y = 2, t = 0.5: f(1) = 1 <=
   0.5 * 0 + 0.5 * 4 = 2. OK. f(x) = x^3 on R is not convex (negative x).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: convexity guarantees that a local minimum found by
   gradient descent is global.
parts.I:
MISTAKE: assuming that a successful training run found the global
   optimum of a non-convex objective.
parts.J:
RELATED: Hessian positive semi-definiteness (F9.5, F12.6),
   regularized objectives, KKT conditions (Appendix D).

sections.title: DERIVATIVES, GRADIENTS AND OPTIMALITY CONDITIONS

blocks.rawText:
Recap (Modules 3 and 12):
   FIRST-ORDER NECESSARY CONDITION: at an interior local minimum of a
      differentiable f, the gradient is zero: grad f(theta*) = 0 (a
      stationary point).
   SECOND-ORDER SUFFICIENT CONDITION: if grad f(theta*) = 0 and the Hessian
      H(theta*) is positive definite, theta* is a strict local minimum;
      negative definite: local maximum; indefinite: saddle point.
   For CONVEX f, grad f = 0 is necessary AND sufficient for a global
   minimum.
   GRADIENT: grad f points to steepest ascent; -grad f is the steepest descent
   direction; |grad f| is the slope in that direction.
EXAMPLE: f(x, y) = (x - 1)^2 + 2 (y + 2)^2: grad f = (2(x - 1), 4(y + 2)) = 0
   at (1, -2); Hessian diag(2, 4) positive definite: strict (global)
   minimum, f = 0.
   FINITE-DIFFERENCE GRADIENT (when no formula is available):
      df/dx approx ( f(x + h) - f(x - h) )/(2h), error of order h^2 (use
      h around 1e-5 for float64). Check: f(x) = e^x sin x at x = 1 has
      derivative e (sin 1 + cos 1) = 3.756049; the central difference with
      h = 1e-5 gives 3.756049. Cost: 2 function evaluations per
      parameter. AUTOMATIC DIFFERENTIATION (PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow)
      computes exact gradients using the chain rule (Module 12.4).

sections.title: GRADIENT DESCENT

blocks.title: GRADIENT DESCENT (GD)
blocks.formulaBody:
UPDATE RULE
     theta_(t+1) = theta_t - eta * grad f(theta_t)
   Stop when |grad f| < tolerance, or the decrease in f is tiny, or a
   maximum number of iterations is reached.

parts.B:
UPDATE RULE
     theta_(t+1) = theta_t - eta * grad f(theta_t)
   Stop when |grad f| < tolerance, or the decrease in f is tiny, or a
   maximum number of iterations is reached.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: theta_t parameter vector at iteration t; eta > 0 the LEARNING RATE
   (step size); grad f(theta_t) the gradient at the current point.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: from the current point, move a small step in the direction
   in which f decreases fastest. Repeat. Like walking downhill in fog,
   using only the slope under your feet.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: f differentiable; eta must be small enough (see below); finds a
   stationary point: global minimum for convex f, otherwise only a local
   minimum or saddle point (43.6). Each iteration costs one gradient.
parts.F:
DERIVATION: first-order Taylor expansion (F5.6, F12.6):
   f(theta + d) approx f(theta) + grad f(theta)^T d. Among steps of fixed length
   |d| = r the decrease is largest for d = -r grad f/|grad f| (Cauchy-
   Schwarz, F10.1), so the steepest-descent step is d = -eta grad f.
   With d = -eta g: f(theta - eta g) approx f(theta) - eta |g|^2 < f(theta) for
   small enough eta.
parts.G:
WORKED EXAMPLES
   (1) ONE VARIABLE: f(x) = x^2, f'(x) = 2x, start x_0 = 4, eta = 0.1.
       x_(t+1) = x_t - 0.1 (2 x_t) = 0.8 x_t.
       x_1 = 3.2; x_2 = 2.56; x_3 = 2.048; ... x_10 = 4 * 0.8^10 = 0.4295.
       The error shrinks by the constant factor 0.8 per step: LINEAR
       (geometric) convergence.
   (2) EFFECT OF THE LEARNING RATE on f(x) = x^2 (update x -> (1 - 2 eta) x),
       start x_0 = 4:
          eta = 0.1: factor 0.8: 4, 3.2, 2.56 ... (steady convergence)
          eta = 0.5: factor 0: 4 -> 0 in ONE step (the ideal for this f)
          eta = 1.0: factor -1: 4, -4, 4, -4 ... (oscillates forever)
          eta = 1.1: factor -1.2: 4, -4.8, 5.76, -6.91, 8.29 ... DIVERGES.
       Rule for f = (a/2) x^2 (f'' = a): converges iff 0 < eta < 2/a.
   (3) TWO VARIABLES, DIFFERENT CURVATURES: f(x, y) = x^2 + 3 y^2, start
       (2, 1), eta = 0.1. grad f = (2x, 6y). Updates:
       x -> 0.8 x, y -> 0.4 y:  (1.6, 0.4), (1.28, 0.16), (1.024, 0.064)...
       Converges, but x (curvature 2) lags behind y (curvature 6).
       Hessian eigenvalues 2 and 6: need eta < 2/6 = 0.333 for stability;
       the best fixed step is eta = 2/(2 + 6) = 0.25, giving factors
       1 - 0.25 * 2 = 0.5 and 1 - 0.25 * 6 = -0.5.
   (4) GENERAL QUADRATIC THEORY: for f = (1/2) theta^T A theta with A symmetric
       positive definite (eigenvalues lambda_min to lambda_max), GD error
       contracts by max_i |1 - eta lambda_i| per step. Converges iff
       eta < 2/lambda_max. The best step eta = 2/(lambda_max + lambda_min)
       gives rate (kappa - 1)/(kappa + 1), with CONDITION NUMBER kappa =
       lambda_max/lambda_min. kappa = 100: rate 0.98 (about 115 iterations to
       gain one more decimal digit); kappa = 1: converges in one step.
       Elongated elliptical contours (large kappa) make GD zig-zag
       (Module 12.1).
   (5) LINEAR REGRESSION BY GD: fit y = c + m t to (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 2)
       (the least-squares example F10.5). Loss L(beta) = (1/(2n)) sum (y_i - c -
       m t_i)^2; gradient = -(1/n) X^T (y - X beta); X = [1 0 ; 1 1 ; 1 2].
       Start beta = (0, 0): residuals (1, 2, 2); gradient = -(1/3)(5, 6)
       = (-1.667, -2.0). With eta = 0.1: beta_1 = (0.1667, 0.2).
       Iterations (c, m) and loss: 
         t=1 (0.1667, 0.2000) loss 0.9028
         t=2 (0.2967, 0.3500) loss 0.5555
         t=3 (0.3987, 0.4620) loss 0.3531
         t=4 (0.4793, 0.5451) loss 0.2347
         t=5 (0.5435, 0.6064) loss 0.1651
       After 2,000 iterations: (1.16667, 0.50000): the exact least-squares
       solution from the normal equations. Eigenvalues of X^T X/n are 0.279
       and 2.387 (kappa = 8.55): stable for eta < 2/2.387 = 0.84; the
       slow direction (eigenvalue 0.279) has contraction factor
       1 - 0.1 * 0.279 = 0.972, which is why thousands of iterations are
       needed. (Centering t makes the problem better conditioned and
       faster: feature scaling, Module 42.)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: eta is the most important hyperparameter of GD-trained
   models (Module 47). Loss curves: smooth decrease = good; flat = eta too
   small; zig-zag or increase = eta too large; noisy plateau (SGD) =
   expected.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: learning rate too large; not scaling features (huge
   condition number); stopping criterion too loose or tight; computing
   gradients incorrectly (verify with finite differences, "gradient
   checking"); expecting the global minimum for non-convex losses;
   forgetting to shuffle data in SGD.
parts.J:
RELATED: Euler's method for gradient flow (F16.5), Newton's method (43.4).

GD VARIANTS (for data-science loss functions L(theta) = (1/n) sum L_i(theta))
   BATCH GD: gradient over all n examples; exact, expensive for large n.
   STOCHASTIC GD (SGD): gradient of ONE random example (an unbiased but noisy
      estimate of the full gradient: E[grad L_i] = grad L). Cheap steps,
      noisy path, can escape shallow traps; needs a decreasing learning
      rate to converge exactly (Robbins-Monro conditions: sum eta_t =
      infinity, sum eta_t^2 < infinity, e.g. eta_t proportional to 1/t).
   MINI-BATCH SGD: gradient of a random batch of m examples (m = 32-512):
      the standard compromise (variance of the gradient estimate falls like
      1/m; hardware-friendly).
   MOMENTUM: v <- mu v + grad; theta <- theta - eta v: accumulates a running
      direction, damping zig-zags. ADAPTIVE METHODS (AdaGrad, RMSProp,
      Adam): per-parameter step sizes from gradient statistics.
   LEARNING-RATE SCHEDULES: step decay, exponential decay eta_0 e^(-k t),
      1/t decay, cosine, warm-up; BACKTRACKING LINE SEARCH (Armijo): shrink
      eta until f decreases enough.
CONVERGENCE SUMMARY
   Strongly convex, smooth f, suitable eta: GD converges LINEARLY
   (geometrically) with rate depending on kappa. Convex, not strongly:
   sublinear O(1/t). Non-convex: converges to stationary points only.
   SGD with constant eta converges to a NEIGHBOURHOOD of the optimum.

   gradients incorrectly (verify with finite differences, "gradient
   checking"); expecting the global minimum for non-convex losses;
   forgetting to shuffle data in SGD.
J. RELATED: Euler's method for gradient flow (F16.5), Newton's method (43.4).

GD VARIANTS (for data-science loss functions L(theta) = (1/n) sum L_i(theta))
   BATCH GD: gradient over all n examples; exact, expensive for large n.
   STOCHASTIC GD (SGD): gradient of ONE random example (an unbiased but noisy
      estimate of the full gradient: E[grad L_i] = grad L). Cheap steps,
      noisy path, can escape shallow traps; needs a decreasing learning
      rate to converge exactly (Robbins-Monro conditions: sum eta_t =
      infinity, sum eta_t^2 < infinity, e.g. eta_t proportional to 1/t).
   MINI-BATCH SGD: gradient of a random batch of m examples (m = 32-512):
      the standard compromise (variance of the gradient estimate falls like
      1/m; hardware-friendly).
   MOMENTUM: v <- mu v + grad; theta <- theta - eta v: accumulates a running
      direction, damping zig-zags. ADAPTIVE METHODS (AdaGrad, RMSProp,
      Adam): per-parameter step sizes from gradient statistics.

   (geometrically) with rate depending on kappa. Convex, not strongly:

sections.rawText:
F43.2  GRADIENT DESCENT (GD)
A. NAME: Gradient descent (steepest descent).
B. UPDATE RULE
     theta_(t+1) = theta_t - eta * grad f(theta_t)
   Stop when |grad f| < tolerance, or the decrease in f is tiny, or a
   maximum number of iterations is reached.
C. SYMBOLS: theta_t parameter vector at iteration t; eta > 0 the LEARNING RATE
   (step size); grad f(theta_t) the gradient at the current point.
D. CONCEPT: from the current point, move a small step in the direction
   in which f decreases fastest. Repeat. Like walking downhill in fog,
   using only the slope under your feet.
E. CONDITIONS: f differentiable; eta must be small enough (see below); finds a
   stationary point: global minimum for convex f, otherwise only a local
   minimum or saddle point (43.6). Each iteration costs one gradient.
F. DERIVATION: first-order Taylor expansion (F5.6, F12.6):
   f(theta + d) approx f(theta) + grad f(theta)^T d. Among steps of fixed length
   |d| = r the decrease is largest for d = -r grad f/|grad f| (Cauchy-
   Schwarz, F10.1), so the steepest-descent step is d = -eta grad f.
   With d = -eta g: f(theta - eta g) approx f(theta) - eta |g|^2 < f(theta) for
   small enough eta.
G. WORKED EXAMPLES
   (1) ONE VARIABLE: f(x) = x^2, f'(x) = 2x, start x_0 = 4, eta = 0.1.
       x_(t+1) = x_t - 0.1 (2 x_t) = 0.8 x_t.
       x_1 = 3.2; x_2 = 2.56; x_3 = 2.048; ... x_10 = 4 * 0.8^10 = 0.4295.
       The error shrinks by the constant factor 0.8 per step: LINEAR
       (geometric) convergence.
   (2) EFFECT OF THE LEARNING RATE on f(x) = x^2 (update x -> (1 - 2 eta) x),
       start x_0 = 4:
          eta = 0.1: factor 0.8: 4, 3.2, 2.56 ... (steady convergence)
          eta = 0.5: factor 0: 4 -> 0 in ONE step (the ideal for this f)
          eta = 1.0: factor -1: 4, -4, 4, -4 ... (oscillates forever)
          eta = 1.1: factor -1.2: 4, -4.8, 5.76, -6.91, 8.29 ... DIVERGES.
       Rule for f = (a/2) x^2 (f'' = a): converges iff 0 < eta < 2/a.
   (3) TWO VARIABLES, DIFFERENT CURVATURES: f(x, y) = x^2 + 3 y^2, start
       (2, 1), eta = 0.1. grad f = (2x, 6y). Updates:
       x -> 0.8 x, y -> 0.4 y:  (1.6, 0.4), (1.28, 0.16), (1.024, 0.064)...
       Converges, but x (curvature 2) lags behind y (curvature 6).
       Hessian eigenvalues 2 and 6: need eta < 2/6 = 0.333 for stability;
       the best fixed step is eta = 2/(2 + 6) = 0.25, giving factors
       1 - 0.25 * 2 = 0.5 and 1 - 0.25 * 6 = -0.5.
   (4) GENERAL QUADRATIC THEORY: for f = (1/2) theta^T A theta with A symmetric
       positive definite (eigenvalues lambda_min to lambda_max), GD error
       contracts by max_i |1 - eta lambda_i| per step. Converges iff
       eta < 2/lambda_max. The best step eta = 2/(lambda_max + lambda_min)
       gives rate (kappa - 1)/(kappa + 1), with CONDITION NUMBER kappa =
       lambda_max/lambda_min. kappa = 100: rate 0.98 (about 115 iterations to
       gain one more decimal digit); kappa = 1: converges in one step.
       Elongated elliptical contours (large kappa) make GD zig-zag
       (Module 12.1).
   (5) LINEAR REGRESSION BY GD: fit y = c + m t to (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 2)
       (the least-squares example F10.5). Loss L(beta) = (1/(2n)) sum (y_i - c -
       m t_i)^2; gradient = -(1/n) X^T (y - X beta); X = [1 0 ; 1 1 ; 1 2].
       Start beta = (0, 0): residuals (1, 2, 2); gradient = -(1/3)(5, 6)
       = (-1.667, -2.0). With eta = 0.1: beta_1 = (0.1667, 0.2).
       Iterations (c, m) and loss: 
         t=1 (0.1667, 0.2000) loss 0.9028
         t=2 (0.2967, 0.3500) loss 0.5555
         t=3 (0.3987, 0.4620) loss 0.3531
         t=4 (0.4793, 0.5451) loss 0.2347
         t=5 (0.5435, 0.6064) loss 0.1651
       After 2,000 iterations: (1.16667, 0.50000): the exact least-squares
       solution from the normal equations. Eigenvalues of X^T X/n are 0.279
       and 2.387 (kappa = 8.55): stable for eta < 2/2.387 = 0.84; the
       slow direction (eigenvalue 0.279) has contraction factor
       1 - 0.1 * 0.279 = 0.972, which is why thousands of iterations are
       needed. (Centering t makes the problem better conditioned and
       faster: feature scaling, Module 42.)
H. INTERPRETATION: eta is the most important hyperparameter of GD-trained
   models (Module 47). Loss curves: smooth decrease = good; flat = eta too
   small; zig-zag or increase = eta too large; noisy plateau (SGD) =

blocks.title: NEWTON-RAPHSON FOR ROOT FINDING (ONE VARIABLE)
blocks.formulaBody: x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n)    (solves f(x) = 0)

parts.B: FORMULA:   x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n)    (solves f(x) = 0)
parts.C: SYMBOLS: x_n current guess; f'(x_n) the slope there.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: replace f by its tangent line at x_n (F3.2) and jump to where the
   tangent crosses the x-axis.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: f'(x_n) != 0; start reasonably close to the root; convergence
   is QUADRATIC near a simple root (the number of correct digits roughly
   doubles each step). Can diverge, cycle, or jump to another root
   from a poor start.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: solve x^2 - 2 = 0 (sqrt 2): x_(n+1) = x_n - (x_n^2 - 2)/(2 x_n)
   = (x_n + 2/x_n)/2. From x_0 = 1: 1.5, 1.416667, 1.4142157, 1.41421356
   (true sqrt 2 = 1.41421356237): errors 0.086, 0.0025, 2 x 10^-6, 2 x
   10^-12: digits double. (Same recursion as the sequence in F5.1.)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the tangent-line jump converges very fast near the
   root.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: starting near a point with f' = 0; expecting
   convergence from any start.
parts.J:
RELATED: bisection and IVT (F2.7), Newton for optimization (F43.4),
   the sequence in F5.1.

blocks.title: NEWTON'S METHOD FOR OPTIMIZATION (MULTIVARIATE)
blocks.formulaBody:
theta_(t+1) = theta_t - H(theta_t)^(-1) grad f(theta_t)
   implemented by SOLVING  H d = -grad f  for the step d (never by forming
   the inverse), then theta <- theta + d. In one variable:
   x_(n+1) = x_n - f'(x_n)/f''(x_n) (root finding applied to f' = 0).

parts.A: NAME: Newton's method (Newton-Raphson applied to the gradient).
parts.B:
FORMULA
     theta_(t+1) = theta_t - H(theta_t)^(-1) grad f(theta_t)
   implemented by SOLVING  H d = -grad f  for the step d (never by forming
   the inverse), then theta <- theta + d. In one variable:
   x_(n+1) = x_n - f'(x_n)/f''(x_n) (root finding applied to f' = 0).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: H the Hessian matrix of second partial derivatives (F12.6).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: approximate f by its SECOND-order Taylor model
   q(d) = f + g^T d + (1/2) d^T H d and jump to that quadratic's minimizer
   d = -H^(-1) g. The Hessian supplies curvature: flat directions take
   LONG steps, steep directions SHORT steps, so the step size adapts
   automatically (no learning rate; well-conditioned in the right
   coordinates).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: needs the Hessian (expensive: d^2 entries, O(d^3) to solve);
   the Hessian must be positive definite near the solution, otherwise
   the step may point uphill or toward a saddle (modify H: add lambda I,
   trust regions, line search). Pure Newton may diverge far from the
   optimum. Local convergence is quadratic.
   Practical variants: QUASI-NEWTON (BFGS, L-BFGS build a Hessian
   approximation from gradients), Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt
   (nonlinear least squares), IRLS (logistic regression).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Quadratic in two variables: f = x^2 + 3 y^2 from (2, 1): g = (4, 6);
      H = diag(2, 6); step d = -H^(-1) g = -(2, 1): new point (0, 0)
      exactly in ONE step (Newton solves quadratics in one step; GD needed
      many).
   One variable: minimize f(x) = x - ln x (x > 0): f' = 1 - 1/x, f'' = 1/x^2.
      Newton: x_(n+1) = x - (1 - 1/x) x^2 = 2x - x^2. From x_0 = 0.5:
      0.75, 0.9375, 0.99609, 0.9999847, 0.99999999977. The distance to the
      minimizer x = 1 is 0.25, 0.0625, 0.0039, 1.5 x 10^-5, 2.3 x 10^-10:
      each error is the SQUARE of the previous (quadratic convergence).
   Logistic regression: Newton/IRLS typically converges in 5-10 iterations.
parts.H: INTERPRETATION: Newton uses curvature; GD uses only slope.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: inverting H explicitly; applying Newton where H is not
   positive definite (a maximum or saddle attracts it); divide-by-zero
   when f'' = 0; using it for huge parameter counts (neural nets).
parts.J:
RELATED: gradient descent (F43.2), BFGS and L-BFGS, IRLS for logistic
   regression.

blocks.title: COMPARISON TABLE: GRADIENT DESCENT vs NEWTON'S METHOD
blocks.rawText:
Aspect                Gradient descent               Newton's method
  Information used      gradient (first order)         gradient + Hessian (second order)
  Update                theta - eta g                  theta - H^(-1) g
  Step size             needs tuned eta                determined by curvature
  Cost per iteration    O(d) (one gradient)            O(d^2) memory, O(d^3) solve
  Iterations needed     many (linear rate, depends     few (quadratic rate near solution)
                        on kappa)
  Convergence           global for small eta (convex)  local; may diverge from poor start
  Sensitive to scale    yes (condition number)         invariant to linear rescaling
  Non-convex behavior   moves downhill always          may move toward saddles/maxima
  Large-scale use       standard (SGD, Adam)           limited; use L-BFGS / quasi-Newton
  Example               training neural nets           logistic regression (IRLS),
                                                       small/medium smooth problems

sections.title: NELDER-MEAD METHOD

blocks.title: NELDER-MEAD (DOWNHILL SIMPLEX)
blocks.formulaBody:
IDEA AND ALGORITHM: a DERIVATIVE-FREE method. In n dimensions keep a SIMPLEX
   of n + 1 points (a triangle in 2D, tetrahedron in 3D). Each iteration:
     1. ORDER the vertices by f: best x_1, ..., worst x_(n+1).
     2. Compute the CENTROID c of all vertices except the worst.
     3. REFLECT the worst through the centroid: x_r = c + alpha (c - x_worst)
        (standard alpha = 1).
     4. If x_r is better than the best: try EXPANSION x_e = c + gamma (x_r - c)
        (gamma = 2); keep the better of x_e and x_r.
        If x_r is between the best and the second-worst: ACCEPT it.
        If x_r is worse than the second-worst: CONTRACT toward the centroid
        (x_c = c + rho (x_worst - c) or c + rho (x_r - c), rho = 0.5); accept
        if better than the worst.
     5. If contraction fails: SHRINK all vertices toward the best:
        x_i <- x_1 + sigma (x_i - x_1) (sigma = 0.5).
     6. Stop when the simplex is small and f values are close.

parts.B:
IDEA AND ALGORITHM: a DERIVATIVE-FREE method. In n dimensions keep a SIMPLEX
   of n + 1 points (a triangle in 2D, tetrahedron in 3D). Each iteration:

sections.title: LOCAL vs GLOBAL MINIMA

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITIONS
   GLOBAL minimum: the lowest value of f over the whole feasible set.
   LOCAL minimum: lowest in a neighbourhood only.
   SADDLE POINT: gradient zero, but the Hessian is indefinite (a minimum in
   some directions, a maximum in others). PLATEAU: a flat region with
   tiny gradient (slow progress).
   Gradient-based methods can only guarantee reaching a STATIONARY point.
WORKED EXAMPLE (non-convex): f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + x, f'(x) = 4x^3 - 6x + 1.
   Stationary points (roots of f'): x = -1.3008 (f = -3.514, GLOBAL minimum),
   x = 0.1699 (f = 0.084, a local MAXIMUM) and x = 1.1309 (f = -1.070,
   a LOCAL minimum, not global).
   Gradient descent with eta = 0.01 (500 iterations): from x_0 = 2 it converges to
   1.1309 (stuck in the local minimum, f = -1.07); from x_0 = -2 it converges
   to -1.3008 (the global minimum, f = -3.51). THE ANSWER DEPENDS ON THE
   START.
SADDLE EXAMPLE: f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2: gradient (2x, -2y) vanishes at the
   origin; Hessian diag(2, -2) indefinite. GD (eta = 0.1) starting at
   (1, 0) converges to (0, 0) (the saddle) because y stays exactly 0; a tiny
   perturbation (1, 10^-6) escapes: y grows by 1.2 per step (and f is
   unbounded below). In high dimensions saddles are far more common than
   local minima; SGD noise and momentum help escape them.
STRATEGIES FOR NON-CONVEX PROBLEMS: multiple random restarts and keep the
   best; sensible initialization; stochastic noise (SGD); momentum/adaptive
   methods; simulated annealing; evolutionary/genetic algorithms;
   convex relaxations; regularization to smooth the landscape. For
   neural networks many local minima give similarly good test
   performance, so exact global optimality is rarely needed.
GUARANTEES: convex + differentiable => any stationary point is a global
   minimum; strictly convex => unique. Linear regression and logistic
   regression objectives are convex; k-means, mixture models and deep
   networks are not.
CHECKS: plot loss versus iteration; try several initializations; compare
the final value across runs.

sections.title: NUMERICAL OPTIMIZATION IN PRACTICE; CONVERGENCE

blocks.rawText:
CONVERGENCE CRITERIA: |grad f| < tol_g; |theta_(t+1) - theta_t| < tol_x;
   |f_t - f_(t+1)| < tol_f (absolute or relative); maximum iterations.
   Always inspect WHY the optimizer stopped (result.message, result.success).
PRACTICAL ISSUES: scaling/conditioning (standardize features, Module 42);
   floating-point error; ill-posed problems (collinearity: flat valleys,
   Module 40.6); choice of starting point; noisy gradients; constraints
   (bounds, equality/inequality): use projected GD, penalty/barrier
   methods, Lagrange multipliers (F12.8), or solvers such as L-BFGS-B, SLSQP.
SCIPY QUICK REFERENCE (verified on Rosenbrock)
   from scipy import optimize
   rosen = lambda p: (1 - p[0])**2 + 100*(p[1] - p[0]**2)**2
   res = optimize.minimize(rosen, x0=[-1.2, 1], method="BFGS")
   res.x -> [0.99999328, 0.99998655]; res.fun -> 4.5e-11; res.nit -> 31;
   res.success, res.message
   optimize.minimize(..., jac=grad_function)   # supply exact gradients
   methods: "BFGS", "L-BFGS-B" (large, bounded), "CG", "Newton-CG",
            "Nelder-Mead", "Powell" (derivative-free), "SLSQP"/"trust-constr"
            (constraints).
   optimize.minimize_scalar(f, bounds=(a, b), method="bounded")  # 1D
   optimize.root(f, x0) / brentq (root finding); optimize.curve_fit and
   least_squares (nonlinear regression).
SIMPLE GD IN PYTHON
   def gradient_descent(grad, theta0, eta=0.1, tol=1e-8, max_iter=10000):
       theta = np.array(theta0, dtype=float)
       for t in range(max_iter):
           g = grad(theta)
           if np.linalg.norm(g) < tol: break
           theta = theta - eta * g
       return theta, t
   X = np.array([[1, 0], [1, 1], [1, 2.]]); y = np.array([1, 2, 2.])
   grad = lambda b: -(X.T @ (y - X @ b)) / len(y)
   gradient_descent(grad, [0, 0])  ->  beta about [1.16667, 0.5]

sections.title: OPTIMIZATION IN REGRESSION

blocks.rawText:
LINEAR REGRESSION (convex quadratic objective)
   Objective: L(beta) = (1/(2n)) |y - X beta|^2; gradient -(1/n) X^T (y - X
   beta); Hessian (1/n) X^T X (PSD).
   Solutions: (1) closed form via normal equations beta = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y;
   computed in practice by QR or SVD (Module 10), cost O(n p^2); (2) GD/SGD,
   cost O(n p) per full-gradient step, preferable when p or n is huge or
   data arrive in streams; (3) Newton converges in ONE step (quadratic
   objective).
RIDGE REGRESSION: minimize |y - X beta|^2 + lambda |beta|^2: gradient adds
   2 lambda beta; closed form (X^T X + lambda I)^(-1) X^T y (Modules 9, 47): the
   added lambda I removes singularity and improves conditioning (every
   eigenvalue increases by lambda, so kappa shrinks).
LASSO: adds lambda |beta|_1: not differentiable at 0; solved by coordinate
   descent or proximal/sub-gradient methods; yields exact zeros (feature
   selection).
LOGISTIC REGRESSION: minimize the average negative Bernoulli log-likelihood
   L(beta) = -(1/n) sum [y_i ln p_i + (1 - y_i) ln(1 - p_i)], p_i =
   sigma(x_i^T beta), sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^(-z)).
   Gradient: (1/n) X^T (p - y); Hessian: (1/n) X^T W X with W = diag(p_i (1 -
   p_i)) (PSD: a CONVEX problem, no local minima). No closed form:
   GD/Newton (IRLS)/L-BFGS.
   WORKED EXAMPLE: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with y = 0, 0, 1, 1; X = [1 x]. At beta =
   (0, 0) every p_i = 0.5; residuals p - y = (0.5, 0.5, -0.5, -0.5);
   gradient = (1/4) X^T (p - y) = (1/4)(0, 0.5 - 1 - 1.5) = (0, -0.5); loss
   = ln 2 = 0.6931. One GD step with eta = 0.1: beta = (0, 0.05): the slope
   becomes positive (larger x -> more likely class 1). 
   !! NOTE !! This particular data set is PERFECTLY SEPARABLE (x <= 1 are all
   class 0; x >= 2 all class 1), so the unpenalized MLE does not exist: the
   coefficients grow without bound while the loss tends to 0. Regularization
   (an L2 penalty) or early stopping fixes this (Module 47). Separation is a
   frequent cause of "non-convergence" warnings.
NEURAL NETWORKS: objectives are non-convex; trained by mini-batch SGD with
   gradients from back-propagation (the chain rule, F12.5).
K-MEANS: alternating minimization of within-cluster squared distance
   (converges to a local minimum; use several random starts).

title: TREE-BASED LEARNING
introRaw:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
A decision tree plays "twenty questions" with the data. It asks a series
of simple yes/no questions about the features ("Is x <= 4.5?"), each
chosen to separate the outcomes as cleanly as possible, until the
groups at the bottom are (nearly) pure. To predict for a new case, you
answer the questions about it and read off the answer at the end of the
path. The mathematical heart of tree learning is the measurement of
how "mixed" a group is (impurity) and how much a question reduces it.

sections.title: STRUCTURE: ROOT, NODES, LEAVES, DECISION RULES

blocks.rawText:
TERMINOLOGY (trees, Module 18/19 applied to learning)
   ROOT NODE: the top node; contains ALL training data.
   INTERNAL (DECISION) NODE: a test on one feature, e.g. x_j <= t (numeric)
      or x_j in {A, B} (categorical); sends each case to the left or right
      child (binary splits are standard in CART).
   BRANCH: outcome of a test. LEAF (TERMINAL) NODE: no further split; holds the
      prediction. DEPTH: number of edges from the root to the deepest leaf.
   SPLIT: the chosen (feature, threshold) pair.
GEOMETRY: each split cuts the feature space with an axis-parallel boundary
   (x_j = t). A tree therefore partitions the space into rectangles
   ("boxes"), one per leaf, and predicts a CONSTANT in each: a
   piecewise-constant function.
DECISION RULES: each root-to-leaf path is an IF-THEN rule: a conjunction (AND,
   Module 23) of the tests along the path.
   Example: IF x <= 4.5 THEN class = 1 (4 of 4 training cases positive);
            IF x > 4.5 THEN class = 0 (4 negative, 2 positive).
   Tree = a set of mutually exclusive, exhaustive rules, hence its
   interpretability.
CLASSIFICATION TREE: leaf predicts a class; REGRESSION TREE: leaf predicts a
number. Same structure, different leaf rule and splitting criterion.
   COMPARISON: classification vs regression
     Target                   categorical          numeric
     Leaf prediction          majority class       mean of the y values in the leaf
     Leaf output (soft)       class proportions    (mean, optionally the variance)
     Impurity measure         Gini / entropy       variance (SSE/MSE)
     Evaluation               accuracy, log-loss   RMSE, MAE

sections.rawText:
TERMINOLOGY (trees, Module 18/19 applied to learning)
   ROOT NODE: the top node; contains ALL training data.
   INTERNAL (DECISION) NODE: a test on one feature, e.g. x_j <= t (numeric)
      or x_j in {A, B} (categorical); sends each case to the left or right
      child (binary splits are standard in CART).
   BRANCH: outcome of a test. LEAF (TERMINAL) NODE: no further split; holds the
      prediction. DEPTH: number of edges from the root to the deepest leaf.
   SPLIT: the chosen (feature, threshold) pair.
GEOMETRY: each split cuts the feature space with an axis-parallel boundary
   (x_j = t). A tree therefore partitions the space into rectangles
   ("boxes"), one per leaf, and predicts a CONSTANT in each: a
   piecewise-constant function.
DECISION RULES: each root-to-leaf path is an IF-THEN rule: a conjunction (AND,
   Module 23) of the tests along the path.
   Example: IF x <= 4.5 THEN class = 1 (4 of 4 training cases positive);
            IF x > 4.5 THEN class = 0 (4 negative, 2 positive).
   Tree = a set of mutually exclusive, exhaustive rules, hence its
   interpretability.
CLASSIFICATION TREE: leaf predicts a class; REGRESSION TREE: leaf predicts a
number. Same structure, different leaf rule and splitting criterion.
   COMPARISON: classification vs regression
     Target                   categorical          numeric
     Leaf prediction          majority class       mean of the y values in the leaf
     Leaf output (soft)       class proportions    (mean, optionally the variance)
     Impurity measure         Gini / entropy       variance (SSE/MSE)
     Evaluation               accuracy, log-loss   RMSE, MAE

sections.title: CLASS PROPORTIONS AND TREE PREDICTIONS

blocks.title: CLASS PROPORTIONS AND PREDICTION
blocks.formulaBody:
For a node containing n observations of which n_k belong to class k
   (k = 1..K):
        p_k = n_k / n          (class proportion, a probability estimate)
   Classification prediction: the MAJORITY class, argmax_k p_k.
   Predicted probabilities: P(class k | x in this leaf) = p_k.
   Regression prediction: y_hat = mean of the y_i in the leaf.

parts.B:
For a node containing n observations of which n_k belong to class k
   (k = 1..K):
        p_k = n_k / n          (class proportion, a probability estimate)
   Classification prediction: the MAJORITY class, argmax_k p_k.
   Predicted probabilities: P(class k | x in this leaf) = p_k.
   Regression prediction: y_hat = mean of the y_i in the leaf.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: n_k count of class k in the node; p_k = n_k/n; sum_k p_k = 1.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the tree treats every case that falls in the same leaf alike, and
   the best constant guess for that group is the group's typical value.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: leaves with few cases give unreliable proportions (a leaf
   with 1 observation says "probability 1.0"): regularize (min samples
   per leaf) or smooth (Laplace correction (n_k + 1)/(n + K)). Predicted
   probabilities from a single deep tree are poorly calibrated.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE (the toy data used below: x = 1..10; labels 1,1,1,1,0,1,0,0,0,1;
   6 positives, 4 negatives): after the split x <= 4.5, the left leaf has 4
   positives, 0 negatives: p(1) = 1.0 -> predict 1. The right leaf has 2
   positives and 4 negatives: p(1) = 1/3 -> predict class 0 with
   probability 2/3 for class 0.
   Prediction for x = 3: path root -> left leaf -> class 1 (p = 1.0). For
   x = 7: path root -> right leaf -> class 0 (p(class 0) = 0.667).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the leaf's majority class is the best guess; the
   proportions express the uncertainty.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: reading leaf proportions as true probabilities when leaves are
   tiny; forgetting that regression trees cannot extrapolate beyond the
   range of leaf means (the prediction never exceeds the training y-range).
parts.J:
RELATED: Gini and entropy (F44.2, F44.3), probability calibration
   (F46.5).

sections.title: SPLITTING CRITERIA: GINI IMPURITY, ENTROPY, INFORMATION GAIN

blocks.rawText:
BASIC IDEA: a node is PURE if all its cases share one class. An impurity
measure is 0 for a pure node and largest for a perfectly mixed node. The
best split is the one that produces the purest children (on average).

blocks.title: GINI IMPURITY
blocks.formulaBody:
G = 1 - sum[k=1..K] p_k^2 = sum[k] p_k (1 - p_k)
   Range: 0 (pure) to 1 - 1/K (all classes equally likely).
   Two classes: G = 2 p (1 - p), maximum 0.5 at p = 0.5.

parts.B:
FORMULA:   G = 1 - sum[k=1..K] p_k^2 = sum[k] p_k (1 - p_k)
   Range: 0 (pure) to 1 - 1/K (all classes equally likely).
   Two classes: G = 2 p (1 - p), maximum 0.5 at p = 0.5.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: p_k class proportions in the node (F44.1); K number of classes.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the probability that two cases drawn at random (with replacement)
   from the node belong to DIFFERENT classes; equivalently, the error rate
   if each case were labeled randomly according to the node's class
   distribution. Lower = purer.
parts.E: CONDITIONS: needs class proportions; for K classes the maximum is 1 - 1/K.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: node with 6 positives and 4 negatives: p = (0.6, 0.4):
      G = 1 - (0.36 + 0.16) = 0.48 (= 2 * 0.6 * 0.4).
   Pure node (4, 0): G = 1 - 1 = 0. Evenly mixed (5, 5): G = 0.5.
   Three classes (0.5, 0.3, 0.2): G = 1 - (0.25 + 0.09 + 0.04) = 0.62
      (maximum 2/3 = 0.667).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: G = 0.48 for a 60/40 node says there is a 48% chance
   that two randomly drawn cases differ in class.
parts.I: MISTAKES: forgetting the "1 -"; using counts instead of proportions.
parts.J:
RELATED: entropy (F44.3), information gain (F44.4), misclassification
   error.

blocks.rawText:
F44.2  GINI IMPURITY
A. NAME: Gini impurity (Gini index).
B. FORMULA:   G = 1 - sum[k=1..K] p_k^2 = sum[k] p_k (1 - p_k)
   Range: 0 (pure) to 1 - 1/K (all classes equally likely).
   Two classes: G = 2 p (1 - p), maximum 0.5 at p = 0.5.
C. SYMBOLS: p_k class proportions in the node (F44.1); K number of classes.
D. CONCEPT: the probability that two cases drawn at random (with replacement)
   from the node belong to DIFFERENT classes; equivalently, the error rate
   if each case were labeled randomly according to the node's class
   distribution. Lower = purer.
E. CONDITIONS: needs class proportions; for K classes the maximum is 1 - 1/K.
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: node with 6 positives and 4 negatives: p = (0.6, 0.4):
      G = 1 - (0.36 + 0.16) = 0.48 (= 2 * 0.6 * 0.4).
   Pure node (4, 0): G = 1 - 1 = 0. Evenly mixed (5, 5): G = 0.5.
   Three classes (0.5, 0.3, 0.2): G = 1 - (0.25 + 0.09 + 0.04) = 0.62

H. INTERPRETATION: G = 0.48 for a 60/40 node says there is a 48% chance

I. MISTAKES: forgetting the "1 -"; using counts instead of proportions.

blocks.title: ENTROPY
blocks.formulaBody:
H = - sum[k=1..K] p_k log2(p_k),   with the convention 0 log 0 = 0.
   Units: BITS with log base 2 (natural log gives nats; the choice only
   rescales all values by a constant and does not change the best split).
   Range: 0 (pure) to log2 K. Two classes: H = -p log2 p - (1 - p) log2(1 - p),
   maximum 1 bit at p = 0.5.

parts.A: NAME: Shannon entropy of a node.
parts.B:
FORMULA:   H = - sum[k=1..K] p_k log2(p_k),   with the convention 0 log 0 = 0.
   Units: BITS with log base 2 (natural log gives nats; the choice only
   rescales all values by a constant and does not change the best split).
   Range: 0 (pure) to log2 K. Two classes: H = -p log2 p - (1 - p) log2(1 - p),
   maximum 1 bit at p = 0.5.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: p_k class proportions; log2 the base-2 logarithm (F1.12).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the average number of yes/no questions (bits) needed to identify
   the class of a randomly drawn case, i.e. the expected "surprise" or
   uncertainty. Highly uncertain nodes have high entropy. (Information
   theory; cross-entropy loss in Module 48 is a relative.)
parts.E: CONDITIONS: p_k = 0 terms contribute 0.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: 0.971 bits means that almost one full yes/no question
   of uncertainty remains.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: using log base 10 inconsistently; forgetting that log2 of a
   fraction is negative (hence the leading minus); computing 0 * log 0
   as NaN.
parts.J: RELATED: Gini (F44.2), cross-entropy loss (F46.5, Appendix D).

blocks.rawText:
F44.3  ENTROPY
A. NAME: Shannon entropy of a node.
B. FORMULA:   H = - sum[k=1..K] p_k log2(p_k),   with the convention 0 log 0 = 0.
   Units: BITS with log base 2 (natural log gives nats; the choice only
   rescales all values by a constant and does not change the best split).
   Range: 0 (pure) to log2 K. Two classes: H = -p log2 p - (1 - p) log2(1 - p),
   maximum 1 bit at p = 0.5.
C. SYMBOLS: p_k class proportions; log2 the base-2 logarithm (F1.12).
D. CONCEPT: the average number of yes/no questions (bits) needed to identify
   the class of a randomly drawn case, i.e. the expected "surprise" or
   uncertainty. Highly uncertain nodes have high entropy. (Information
   theory; cross-entropy loss in Module 48 is a relative.)
E. CONDITIONS: p_k = 0 terms contribute 0.
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: (0.6, 0.4): H = -0.6 log2 0.6 - 0.4 log2 0.4 = 0.6(0.737) + 0.4(1.322)
      = 0.442 + 0.529 = 0.971 bits.
   (0.8, 0.2): H = 0.722 bits. (1, 0): H = 0. (0.5, 0.5): H = 1.
   Three classes (0.5, 0.3, 0.2): H = 1.485 bits (maximum log2 3 = 1.585).
   Table (two classes): p = 0.1: Gini 0.18, entropy 0.469; p = 0.2: 0.32,
      0.722; p = 0.3: 0.42, 0.881; p = 0.4: 0.48, 0.971; p = 0.5: 0.5, 1.0.
      Both rise and fall together; entropy is a bit more "curved".
H. INTERPRETATION: 0.971 bits means that almost one full yes/no question
   of uncertainty remains.
I. MISTAKES: using log base 10 inconsistently; forgetting that log2 of a
   fraction is negative (hence the leading minus); computing 0 * log 0
   as NaN.
J. RELATED: Gini (F44.2), cross-entropy loss (F46.5, Appendix D).

blocks.title: INFORMATION GAIN (IMPURITY DECREASE)
blocks.formulaBody:
for a split of a parent node with n cases into children j = 1..m
   with n_j cases each:
        Gain = Impurity(parent) - sum[j] (n_j/n) Impurity(child_j)
   (impurity = entropy H gives information gain; impurity = Gini gives the
   Gini decrease). The second term is the WEIGHTED average impurity of the
   children.

parts.A: NAME: Information gain (for entropy) / impurity decrease (for Gini).
parts.B:
FORMULA: for a split of a parent node with n cases into children j = 1..m
   with n_j cases each:
        Gain = Impurity(parent) - sum[j] (n_j/n) Impurity(child_j)
   (impurity = entropy H gives information gain; impurity = Gini gives the
   Gini decrease). The second term is the WEIGHTED average impurity of the
   children.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: n_j/n the share of cases going to child j (the weight).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: how much uncertainty about the class is removed by learning the
   answer to the question. The weights prevent a tiny pure child from
   making a split look better than it is.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: Gain >= 0 for concave impurities. Gain favours splits
   producing many tiny children (e.g. an ID column): use binary splits,
   minimum leaf sizes, or the gain ratio (C4.5) to counter this.
parts.G:
WORKED EXAMPLE (the same data used throughout): x = 1..10, labels
   1,1,1,1,0,1,0,0,0,1 (6 positive, 4 negative):
     Parent: Gini = 0.48; entropy = 0.9710.
   Candidate threshold x <= 4.5 (left = x 1-4: 4 pos, 0 neg; right = x 5-10: 2 pos,
   4 neg):
     Gini left 0; Gini right = 1 - (1/9 + 4/9) = 0.4444.
     Weighted Gini = 0.4 * 0 + 0.6 * 0.4444 = 0.2667; Gini gain =
        0.48 - 0.2667 = 0.2133.
     Entropy right = -(1/3) log2(1/3) - (2/3) log2(2/3) = 0.9183;
     weighted = 0.6 * 0.9183 = 0.5510; Information gain = 0.9710 - 0.5510 =
        0.4200 bits.
   Candidate threshold x <= 5.5 (left 5 cases: 4 pos, 1 neg; right 5 cases: 2 pos,
   3 neg):
     Gini left = 1 - (0.64 + 0.04) = 0.32; right = 1 - (0.16 + 0.36) = 0.48;
     weighted 0.4; Gini gain 0.08.
     Entropy left 0.7219, right 0.9710; weighted 0.8464; information gain
     0.1245 bits.
   All candidate thresholds (midpoints between consecutive x values):
     threshold   left (pos/neg)  right (pos/neg)  weighted Gini  Gini gain  Info. gain
     1.5         1 (1/0)         9 (5/4)          0.4444         0.0356     0.0790
     2.5         2 (2/0)         8 (4/4)          0.4000         0.0800     0.1710
     3.5         3 (3/0)         7 (3/4)          0.3429         0.1371     0.2813
     4.5         4 (4/0)         6 (2/4)          0.2667         0.2133     0.4200
     5.5         5 (4/1)         5 (2/3)          0.4000         0.0800     0.1245
     6.5         6 (5/1)         4 (1/3)          0.3167         0.1633     0.2564
     7.5         7 (5/2)         3 (1/2)          0.4190         0.0610     0.0913
     8.5         8 (5/3)         2 (1/1)          0.4750         0.0050     0.0074
     9.5         9 (5/4)         1 (1/0)          0.4444         0.0356     0.0790
   Best split under BOTH criteria: x <= 4.5. (scikit-learn's
   DecisionTreeClassifier with max_depth=1 returns exactly this tree:
   threshold 4.50, leaves with class counts [0, 4] and [4, 2].)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the first question removes 0.42 of the 0.97 bits of
   uncertainty (43%). Gains are used to rank splits; the sum of gains over
   all splits using a feature gives "impurity-based feature importance".
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: unweighted averaging of child impurities; thinking
   Gini and entropy give very different trees (they usually agree);
   computing gain relative to the wrong parent; considering thresholds
   at data values instead of midpoints (equivalent in effect but check
   the convention).
parts.J: RELATED: entropy and KL divergence (Appendix D); log-loss (Module 48).

blocks.title: COMPARISON TABLE: GINI vs ENTROPY
blocks.rawText:
Aspect            Gini impurity               Entropy / information gain
  Formula           1 - sum p_k^2               -sum p_k log2 p_k
  Maximum (K = 2)   0.5                         1 bit
  Computation       cheaper (no logs)           slightly slower
  Behavior          similar; tends to isolate   tends to produce slightly more
                    the most frequent class     balanced splits
  Default           scikit-learn "gini"         criterion="entropy" or "log_loss"
  Practical effect  usually negligible difference in accuracy
  Misclassification error 1 - max p_k is less sensitive: used for pruning, not for growing.

blocks.title: SPLITTING CRITERION FOR REGRESSION TREES
blocks.formulaBody:
For a node with responses y_i (i in node), impurity = sum of squared
   deviations from the node mean: SSE = sum (y_i - y_bar)^2 (or MSE =
   SSE/n, the variance). Choose the split (j, t) minimizing
        SSE_left + SSE_right,   equivalently maximizing the variance (SSE)
        reduction  SSE_parent - SSE_left - SSE_right.
   Leaf prediction: y_bar of the leaf.

parts.B:
For a node with responses y_i (i in node), impurity = sum of squared
   deviations from the node mean: SSE = sum (y_i - y_bar)^2 (or MSE =
   SSE/n, the variance). Choose the split (j, t) minimizing
        SSE_left + SSE_right,   equivalently maximizing the variance (SSE)
        reduction  SSE_parent - SSE_left - SSE_right.

sections.rawText:
BASIC IDEA: a node is PURE if all its cases share one class. An impurity
measure is 0 for a pure node and largest for a perfectly mixed node. The
best split is the one that produces the purest children (on average).

F44.2  GINI IMPURITY
A. NAME: Gini impurity (Gini index).
B. FORMULA:   G = 1 - sum[k=1..K] p_k^2 = sum[k] p_k (1 - p_k)
   Range: 0 (pure) to 1 - 1/K (all classes equally likely).
   Two classes: G = 2 p (1 - p), maximum 0.5 at p = 0.5.
C. SYMBOLS: p_k class proportions in the node (F44.1); K number of classes.
D. CONCEPT: the probability that two cases drawn at random (with replacement)
   from the node belong to DIFFERENT classes; equivalently, the error rate
   if each case were labeled randomly according to the node's class
   distribution. Lower = purer.
E. CONDITIONS: needs class proportions; for K classes the maximum is 1 - 1/K.
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: node with 6 positives and 4 negatives: p = (0.6, 0.4):
      G = 1 - (0.36 + 0.16) = 0.48 (= 2 * 0.6 * 0.4).
   Pure node (4, 0): G = 1 - 1 = 0. Evenly mixed (5, 5): G = 0.5.
   Three classes (0.5, 0.3, 0.2): G = 1 - (0.25 + 0.09 + 0.04) = 0.62
      (maximum 2/3 = 0.667).
H. INTERPRETATION: G = 0.48 for a 60/40 node says there is a 48% chance
   that two randomly drawn cases differ in class.
I. MISTAKES: forgetting the "1 -"; using counts instead of proportions.
J. RELATED: entropy (F44.3), information gain (F44.4), misclassification
   error.

F44.3  ENTROPY
A. NAME: Shannon entropy of a node.
B. FORMULA:   H = - sum[k=1..K] p_k log2(p_k),   with the convention 0 log 0 = 0.
   Units: BITS with log base 2 (natural log gives nats; the choice only
   rescales all values by a constant and does not change the best split).
   Range: 0 (pure) to log2 K. Two classes: H = -p log2 p - (1 - p) log2(1 - p),
   maximum 1 bit at p = 0.5.
C. SYMBOLS: p_k class proportions; log2 the base-2 logarithm (F1.12).
D. CONCEPT: the average number of yes/no questions (bits) needed to identify
   the class of a randomly drawn case, i.e. the expected "surprise" or
   uncertainty. Highly uncertain nodes have high entropy. (Information
   theory; cross-entropy loss in Module 48 is a relative.)
E. CONDITIONS: p_k = 0 terms contribute 0.
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: (0.6, 0.4): H = -0.6 log2 0.6 - 0.4 log2 0.4 = 0.6(0.737) + 0.4(1.322)
      = 0.442 + 0.529 = 0.971 bits.
   (0.8, 0.2): H = 0.722 bits. (1, 0): H = 0. (0.5, 0.5): H = 1.
   Three classes (0.5, 0.3, 0.2): H = 1.485 bits (maximum log2 3 = 1.585).
   Table (two classes): p = 0.1: Gini 0.18, entropy 0.469; p = 0.2: 0.32,
      0.722; p = 0.3: 0.42, 0.881; p = 0.4: 0.48, 0.971; p = 0.5: 0.5, 1.0.
      Both rise and fall together; entropy is a bit more "curved".
H. INTERPRETATION: 0.971 bits means that almost one full yes/no question
   of uncertainty remains.
I. MISTAKES: using log base 10 inconsistently; forgetting that log2 of a
   fraction is negative (hence the leading minus); computing 0 * log 0
   as NaN.
J. RELATED: Gini (F44.2), cross-entropy loss (F46.5, Appendix D).

F44.4  INFORMATION GAIN (IMPURITY DECREASE)
A. NAME: Information gain (for entropy) / impurity decrease (for Gini).
B. FORMULA: for a split of a parent node with n cases into children j = 1..m
   with n_j cases each:
        Gain = Impurity(parent) - sum[j] (n_j/n) Impurity(child_j)
   (impurity = entropy H gives information gain; impurity = Gini gives the
   Gini decrease). The second term is the WEIGHTED average impurity of the
   children.
C. SYMBOLS: n_j/n the share of cases going to child j (the weight).
D. CONCEPT: how much uncertainty about the class is removed by learning the
   answer to the question. The weights prevent a tiny pure child from
   making a split look better than it is.
E. CONDITIONS: Gain >= 0 for concave impurities. Gain favours splits
   producing many tiny children (e.g. an ID column): use binary splits,
   minimum leaf sizes, or the gain ratio (C4.5) to counter this.
G. WORKED EXAMPLE (the same data used throughout): x = 1..10, labels
   1,1,1,1,0,1,0,0,0,1 (6 positive, 4 negative):
     Parent: Gini = 0.48; entropy = 0.9710.
   Candidate threshold x <= 4.5 (left = x 1-4: 4 pos, 0 neg; right = x 5-10: 2 pos,
   4 neg):
     Gini left 0; Gini right = 1 - (1/9 + 4/9) = 0.4444.
     Weighted Gini = 0.4 * 0 + 0.6 * 0.4444 = 0.2667; Gini gain =
        0.48 - 0.2667 = 0.2133.
     Entropy right = -(1/3) log2(1/3) - (2/3) log2(2/3) = 0.9183;
     weighted = 0.6 * 0.9183 = 0.5510; Information gain = 0.9710 - 0.5510 =
        0.4200 bits.
   Candidate threshold x <= 5.5 (left 5 cases: 4 pos, 1 neg; right 5 cases: 2 pos,
   3 neg):
     Gini left = 1 - (0.64 + 0.04) = 0.32; right = 1 - (0.16 + 0.36) = 0.48;
     weighted 0.4; Gini gain 0.08.
     Entropy left 0.7219, right 0.9710; weighted 0.8464; information gain
     0.1245 bits.
   All candidate thresholds (midpoints between consecutive x values):
     threshold   left (pos/neg)  right (pos/neg)  weighted Gini  Gini gain  Info. gain
     1.5         1 (1/0)         9 (5/4)          0.4444         0.0356     0.0790
     2.5         2 (2/0)         8 (4/4)          0.4000         0.0800     0.1710
     3.5         3 (3/0)         7 (3/4)          0.3429         0.1371     0.2813
     4.5         4 (4/0)         6 (2/4)          0.2667         0.2133     0.4200
     5.5         5 (4/1)         5 (2/3)          0.4000         0.0800     0.1245
     6.5         6 (5/1)         4 (1/3)          0.3167         0.1633     0.2564
     7.5         7 (5/2)         3 (1/2)          0.4190         0.0610     0.0913
     8.5         8 (5/3)         2 (1/1)          0.4750         0.0050     0.0074
     9.5         9 (5/4)         1 (1/0)          0.4444         0.0356     0.0790
   Best split under BOTH criteria: x <= 4.5. (scikit-learn's
   DecisionTreeClassifier with max_depth=1 returns exactly this tree:
   threshold 4.50, leaves with class counts [0, 4] and [4, 2].)
H. INTERPRETATION: the first question removes 0.42 of the 0.97 bits of
   uncertainty (43%). Gains are used to rank splits; the sum of gains over
   all splits using a feature gives "impurity-based feature importance".
I. COMMON MISTAKES: unweighted averaging of child impurities; thinking
   Gini and entropy give very different trees (they usually agree);
   computing gain relative to the wrong parent; considering thresholds
   at data values instead of midpoints (equivalent in effect but check
   the convention).
J. RELATED: entropy and KL divergence (Appendix D); log-loss (Module 48).

COMPARISON TABLE: GINI vs ENTROPY
  Aspect            Gini impurity               Entropy / information gain
  Formula           1 - sum p_k^2               -sum p_k log2 p_k
  Maximum (K = 2)   0.5                         1 bit
  Computation       cheaper (no logs)           slightly slower
  Behavior          similar; tends to isolate   tends to produce slightly more
                    the most frequent class     balanced splits
  Default           scikit-learn "gini"         criterion="entropy" or "log_loss"
  Practical effect  usually negligible difference in accuracy
  Misclassification error 1 - max p_k is less sensitive: used for pruning, not for growing.

sections.title: OVERFITTING AND PRUNING

blocks.rawText:
THE PROBLEM: with no limits a tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure,
so it memorizes the training data (training accuracy 100%), including the
noise: HIGH VARIANCE, poor generalization (Module 46).
   Toy data fully grown: the tree needs 5 leaves and depth 4 to reach
   training accuracy 1.0, isolating individual points:
      x <= 4.5 -> class 1 [0, 4];
      x > 4.5: x <= 9.5 -> (x <= 6.5 -> (x <= 5.5 -> class 0, else class 1),
      else class 0), x > 9.5 -> class 1.
   The splits at 5.5, 6.5 and 9.5 fit single points (x = 6 and x = 10
   labeled positive among negatives): likely noise.
EXPERIMENT (verified; synthetic data, scikit-learn 1.9):
   make_classification(n_samples = 600, n_features = 10, n_informative = 4,
   n_redundant = 2, flip_y = 0.1, class_sep = 1.0, random_state = 0), stratified
   70/30 split (random_state = 0), DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth = d):
     max_depth   train accuracy   test accuracy   leaves
        1           0.707            0.756            2
        2           0.781            0.739            4
        3           0.874            0.811            8
        4           0.931            0.861           12
        5           0.952            0.867           16
        8           0.979            0.856           28
       12 (full)    1.000            0.872           36
     Reading: depth 1-2 UNDERFIT (low training and test accuracy: high
     bias). Training accuracy keeps rising to 1.0 while the test accuracy
     levels off near 0.86-0.87: the gap (0.128 for the full tree) measures
     overfitting. Here the full tree is not catastrophically worse on test
     data, but it is far more complex (36 leaves) for no gain; with noisier
     data the test accuracy would fall.
CONTROLLING COMPLEXITY
   PRE-PRUNING (early stopping; hyperparameters): max_depth, min_samples_split,
      min_samples_leaf, max_leaf_nodes, min_impurity_decrease. Simple and
      fast, but may stop too early (a poor first split can hide a good
      second split).
   POST-PRUNING: grow a large tree, then cut back. COST-COMPLEXITY (weakest-
      link) PRUNING:

blocks.title: COST-COMPLEXITY PRUNING
blocks.formulaBody:
R_alpha(T) = R(T) + alpha |T|
   R(T): training error (misclassification rate or impurity) of tree T;
   |T|: number of leaves; alpha >= 0: the complexity penalty per leaf.
   For each alpha there is a unique smallest subtree minimizing R_alpha; as
   alpha increases the tree shrinks (alpha = 0: the full tree; large alpha:
   the root only). Choose alpha by CROSS-VALIDATION (Module 46/47).

parts.B:
R_alpha(T) = R(T) + alpha |T|
   R(T): training error (misclassification rate or impurity) of tree T;
   |T|: number of leaves; alpha >= 0: the complexity penalty per leaf.
   For each alpha there is a unique smallest subtree minimizing R_alpha; as
   alpha increases the tree shrinks (alpha = 0: the full tree; large alpha:
   the root only). Choose alpha by CROSS-VALIDATION (Module 46/47).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: R(T) the training error; |T| the number of leaves; alpha the
   penalty; T_alpha the best subtree for alpha.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: trade fit against size (Occam's razor); like L1 regularization on
   the number of leaves.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: alpha is chosen by cross-validation; the nested sequence
   of subtrees comes from weakest-link pruning.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE (same experiment, 5-fold CV on the training set, ccp_alpha):
     alpha     CV accuracy   leaves   test accuracy
     0.00000     0.888        36        0.872
     0.00397     0.890        22        0.878
     0.00449     0.886        14        0.889
     0.01161     0.893         8        0.878
     0.02473     0.881         6        0.867
     0.04403     0.838         4        0.817
     0.10290     0.643         2        0.756
   The CV accuracy is essentially flat from 36 down to 8 leaves (0.888 to
   0.893): a much smaller tree does just as well, and is easier to
   interpret; cutting too far (2-4 leaves) hurts. (Differences of a few
   hundredths are within noise on 600 observations.)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: alpha is the price per leaf: higher alpha gives a
   smaller tree.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: choosing the tree size by training error (always favours the full
   tree); tuning ccp_alpha on the test set; ignoring that a pruned tree can
   still be unstable.
parts.J:
RELATED: regularization (section 43.8, F48.7), cross-validation
   (F46.2).
BIAS-VARIANCE VIEW: shallow tree = high bias, low variance; deep tree = low
bias, high variance; pruning trades them. A tiny change in the training
data can change the top split and thus the whole tree (instability): the
motivation for ensembles (Module 45).

bias, high variance; pruning trades them. A tiny change in the training
data can change the top split and thus the whole tree (instability): the
motivation for ensembles (Module 45).

ADVANTAGES AND LIMITATIONS OF DECISION TREES
   + Easy to interpret and visualize (rules); handle numeric and categorical
     features and (in some implementations) missing values; need no feature
     scaling; invariant to monotone transformations of features; capture
     nonlinearities and INTERACTIONS automatically (a split on x_2 inside a
     branch of x_1 = an x_1 by x_2 interaction); fast prediction.
   - High variance/unstable; greedy; axis-parallel boundaries (a diagonal
     boundary needs a staircase of many splits); piecewise-constant
     (no extrapolation, coarse for smooth relationships); biased toward
     features with many possible splits (high cardinality); poor
     probability calibration; class imbalance needs weights.
FEATURE IMPORTANCE (impurity-based): for feature j, sum the (weighted)
   impurity decreases of all splits on j, normalized to sum to 1. Fast but
   biased toward high-cardinality/continuous features and computed on the
   training data; prefer PERMUTATION importance on held-out data (shuffle a
   feature, measure the drop in score).

blocks.text:
trees are the base learner of random forests and gradient
boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM), which dominate tabular-data competitions.
Decision-tree rules also explain model behavior (surrogate models).
PYTHON
   from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
   tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5, ccp_alpha=0.0,
                                 random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
   print(export_text(tree, feature_names=names, show_weights=True))
   tree.predict_proba(X_new); tree.feature_importances_; tree.get_depth()
   tree.cost_complexity_pruning_path(X_train, y_train)  # candidate alphas

        4           0.931            0.861           12
        5           0.952            0.867           16
        8           0.979            0.856           28
       12 (full)    1.000            0.872           36
     Reading: depth 1-2 UNDERFIT (low training and test accuracy: high
     bias). Training accuracy keeps rising to 1.0 while the test accuracy
     levels off near 0.86-0.87: the gap (0.128 for the full tree) measures
     overfitting. Here the full tree is not catastrophically worse on test
     data, but it is far more complex (36 leaves) for no gain; with noisier
     data the test accuracy would fall.
CONTROLLING COMPLEXITY
   PRE-PRUNING (early stopping; hyperparameters): max_depth, min_samples_split,
      min_samples_leaf, max_leaf_nodes, min_impurity_decrease. Simple and
      fast, but may stop too early (a poor first split can hide a good
      second split).
   POST-PRUNING: grow a large tree, then cut back. COST-COMPLEXITY (weakest-
      link) PRUNING:
F44.6  COST-COMPLEXITY PRUNING
B. R_alpha(T) = R(T) + alpha |T|
   R(T): training error (misclassification rate or impurity) of tree T;
   |T|: number of leaves; alpha >= 0: the complexity penalty per leaf.
   For each alpha there is a unique smallest subtree minimizing R_alpha; as
   alpha increases the tree shrinks (alpha = 0: the full tree; large alpha:
   the root only). Choose alpha by CROSS-VALIDATION (Module 46/47).
C. SYMBOLS: R(T) the training error; |T| the number of leaves; alpha the
   penalty; T_alpha the best subtree for alpha.
D. CONCEPT: trade fit against size (Occam's razor); like L1 regularization on
   the number of leaves.
E. CONDITIONS: alpha is chosen by cross-validation; the nested sequence
   of subtrees comes from weakest-link pruning.
G. EXAMPLE (same experiment, 5-fold CV on the training set, ccp_alpha):
     alpha     CV accuracy   leaves   test accuracy
     0.00000     0.888        36        0.872
     0.00397     0.890        22        0.878
     0.00449     0.886        14        0.889
     0.01161     0.893         8        0.878
     0.02473     0.881         6        0.867
     0.04403     0.838         4        0.817
     0.10290     0.643         2        0.756
   The CV accuracy is essentially flat from 36 down to 8 leaves (0.888 to
   0.893): a much smaller tree does just as well, and is easier to
   interpret; cutting too far (2-4 leaves) hurts. (Differences of a few
   hundredths are within noise on 600 observations.)
H. INTERPRETATION: alpha is the price per leaf: higher alpha gives a
   smaller tree.
I. MISTAKES: choosing the tree size by training error (always favours the full
   tree); tuning ccp_alpha on the test set; ignoring that a pruned tree can
   still be unstable.
J. RELATED: regularization (section 43.8, F48.7), cross-validation
   (F46.2).
BIAS-VARIANCE VIEW: shallow tree = high bias, low variance; deep tree = low
bias, high variance; pruning trades them. A tiny change in the training
data can change the top split and thus the whole tree (instability): the
motivation for ensembles (Module 45).

ADVANTAGES AND LIMITATIONS OF DECISION TREES
   + Easy to interpret and visualize (rules); handle numeric and categorical
     features and (in some implementations) missing values; need no feature
     scaling; invariant to monotone transformations of features; capture
     nonlinearities and INTERACTIONS automatically (a split on x_2 inside a
     branch of x_1 = an x_1 by x_2 interaction); fast prediction.
   - High variance/unstable; greedy; axis-parallel boundaries (a diagonal
     boundary needs a staircase of many splits); piecewise-constant
     (no extrapolation, coarse for smooth relationships); biased toward
     features with many possible splits (high cardinality); poor
     probability calibration; class imbalance needs weights.
FEATURE IMPORTANCE (impurity-based): for feature j, sum the (weighted)
   impurity decreases of all splits on j, normalized to sum to 1. Fast but
   biased toward high-cardinality/continuous features and computed on the
   training data; prefer PERMUTATION importance on held-out data (shuffle a
   feature, measure the drop in score).
DATA SCIENCE LINK: trees are the base learner of random forests and gradient
boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM), which dominate tabular-data competitions.
Decision-tree rules also explain model behavior (surrogate models).
PYTHON
   from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
   tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=5, ccp_alpha=0.0,
                                 random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
   print(export_text(tree, feature_names=names, show_weights=True))
   tree.predict_proba(X_new); tree.feature_importances_; tree.get_depth()
   tree.cost_complexity_pruning_path(X_train, y_train)  # candidate alphas

title: RANDOM FORESTS
introRaw:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
One decision tree is unstable: a small change in the data can change it a
lot. But if you grow MANY different trees and let them vote, the
individual mistakes tend to cancel out: the "wisdom of crowds". A random
forest makes the trees different by giving each its own random resample of
the data and by letting each split see only a random subset of the
features.
