sections.title: DECISION TREES vs LINEAR CLASSIFIERS

blocks.rawText:
GEOMETRY
   Linear classifier: ONE oblique hyperplane (any orientation), global
      structure, few parameters (p + 1), extrapolates linearly.
   Decision tree: a union of AXIS-PARALLEL rectangles; local, piecewise
      constant; many parameters (one per leaf), cannot represent an
      oblique boundary except as a staircase.
VERIFIED EXPERIMENT (2,000 uniformly distributed points in a square, 5% of
labels flipped at random so the best possible accuracy is about 0.95; 50/50
train/test split; accuracy on the test half):
   Boundary shape        logistic   tree d=2   tree d=3   full tree (leaves)   RBF SVM
   Diagonal (x1 + x2>0)    0.941      0.834      0.849      0.870 (120)         0.933
   XOR quadrants           0.418      0.536      0.860      0.887 (104)         0.927
   Circle (x1^2+x2^2<1)    0.630      0.702      0.795      0.879 (103)         0.930
   READING:
   - DIAGONAL boundary: the linear model is nearly perfect (0.94); the tree
     must approximate the line with a staircase: even 120 leaves (0.870)
     do worse than 3 numbers in the logistic model. Shallow trees are poor.
   - XOR quadrants: the linear model is no better than chance (0.42 here, a
     fluctuation around 0.5); a depth-3 tree already reaches 0.86 because
     the pattern is axis-aligned rectangles.
   - CIRCLE: curved boundary: linear fails (0.63); trees approximate it with
     many rectangles; the RBF kernel captures it smoothly.
   - The RBF SVM is good for all three shapes (0.93) because it is flexible
     and smooth.

blocks.title: COMPARISON TABLE: DECISION TREES vs LINEAR CLASSIFIERS
blocks.rawText:
Aspect                  Decision tree/forest           Linear (logistic, LDA, lin. SVM)
  Boundary                axis-parallel boxes            one hyperplane
  Interactions            captured automatically         need explicit product terms
  Oblique boundaries      poor (staircase)               natural
  Nonlinear effects       yes (piecewise constant)       need transformations
  Feature scaling         not needed                     needed (regularized models)
  Interpretability        rules (tree); forest: low      coefficients, odds ratios
  Variance                high (single tree)             low (few parameters)
  Data requirement        more data for complex shapes   works with little data
  High dimension, p > n   can overfit, still works       works with regularization
  Extrapolation           constant beyond the data       linear continuation
  Probability output      step functions, uncalibrated   smooth (logistic)
  Missing values/types    handles mixed types, outliers  needs encoding/imputation
  Best when               tabular data, interactions,    approximately linear, many
                          mixed types                    features, small n, need coefficients
  Rule of thumb: start with a regularized linear baseline; try forests/boosting
  for tabular nonlinearity; kernels/NNs for smooth nonlinear structure.

sections.title: LINEAR DISCRIMINANT ANALYSIS (LDA)

blocks.title: LINEAR DISCRIMINANT ANALYSIS
blocks.formulaBody:
Assumptions: within each class k the features are multivariate normal
        x | class k ~ N(mu_k, Sigma)  with the SAME covariance Sigma for all
        classes; prior class probabilities pi_k.
     Bayes' theorem (F34.5): P(k | x) proportional to pi_k N(x; mu_k, Sigma).
     LINEAR DISCRIMINANT FUNCTION for class k:
        delta_k(x) = x^T Sigma^(-1) mu_k - (1/2) mu_k^T Sigma^(-1) mu_k + ln pi_k
     Classify to argmax_k delta_k(x).
     Two classes: predict class 1 if  w^T x + b > 0  with
        w = Sigma^(-1) (mu_1 - mu_0),
        b = -(1/2)(mu_1 + mu_0)^T Sigma^(-1)(mu_1 - mu_0) + ln(pi_1/pi_0).
     ESTIMATION: pi_k = n_k/n; mu_k = class sample mean; Sigma = POOLED within-
        class covariance = sum_k sum_(i in k) (x_i - mu_k)(x_i - mu_k)^T/(n - K).
     FISHER'S CRITERION (equivalent two-class view): find the direction w
        maximizing J(w) = ( w^T (mu_1 - mu_0) )^2 / ( w^T S_W w ), (squared distance
        between projected class means over within-class scatter); the
        solution is w proportional to S_W^(-1)(mu_1 - mu_0).
     Dimension reduction: K - 1 discriminant directions at most.

parts.B:
MODEL AND FORMULAS
     Assumptions: within each class k the features are multivariate normal
        x | class k ~ N(mu_k, Sigma)  with the SAME covariance Sigma for all
        classes; prior class probabilities pi_k.
     Bayes' theorem (F34.5): P(k | x) proportional to pi_k N(x; mu_k, Sigma).
     LINEAR DISCRIMINANT FUNCTION for class k:
        delta_k(x) = x^T Sigma^(-1) mu_k - (1/2) mu_k^T Sigma^(-1) mu_k + ln pi_k
     Classify to argmax_k delta_k(x).
     Two classes: predict class 1 if  w^T x + b > 0  with
        w = Sigma^(-1) (mu_1 - mu_0),
        b = -(1/2)(mu_1 + mu_0)^T Sigma^(-1)(mu_1 - mu_0) + ln(pi_1/pi_0).
     ESTIMATION: pi_k = n_k/n; mu_k = class sample mean; Sigma = POOLED within-
        class covariance = sum_k sum_(i in k) (x_i - mu_k)(x_i - mu_k)^T/(n - K).
     FISHER'S CRITERION (equivalent two-class view): find the direction w
        maximizing J(w) = ( w^T (mu_1 - mu_0) )^2 / ( w^T S_W w ), (squared distance
        between projected class means over within-class scatter); the
        solution is w proportional to S_W^(-1)(mu_1 - mu_0).
     Dimension reduction: K - 1 discriminant directions at most.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the boundary is placed between the class means, adjusted for the
   shape of the (common) covariance: directions where the data are very
   spread contribute less; the priors shift the boundary toward the less
   likely class. Whitening (multiplying by Sigma^(-1/2)) turns the problem
   into "nearest class mean" in a spherical space.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: Gaussian classes with equal covariances (checked by
   within-class scatter plots, Box's M test, or just by performance);
   n > p (or use SHRINKAGE: solver = "lsqr", shrinkage = "auto"); sensitive
   to outliers; linear boundary. If covariances differ: QUADRATIC
   DISCRIMINANT ANALYSIS (QDA): class-specific Sigma_k, boundaries are
   quadratic curves, more parameters, needs more data.
parts.F:
DERIVATION (two classes): ln[ P(1 | x)/P(0 | x) ] = ln(pi_1/pi_0) + ln N(x; mu_1, Sigma)
   - ln N(x; mu_0, Sigma). The Gaussian log-density is -(1/2)(x - mu)^T Sigma^(-1)
   (x - mu) + constant; expanding the quadratic form, the term x^T Sigma^(-1) x
   is the same for both classes and cancels, leaving a LINEAR function
   of x. Setting it to zero gives w and b above.
parts.G:
WORKED EXAMPLES
   Simple: mu_0 = (0, 0), mu_1 = (2, 2), Sigma = I (identity), equal priors:
      w = mu_1 - mu_0 = (2, 2); b = -(1/2)(2, 2).(2, 2) = -4: boundary 2 x_1 + 2 x_2
      = 4, i.e. x_1 + x_2 = 2: the perpendicular bisector of the segment
      joining the means.
   Moderate: Sigma = diag(1, 4) (feature 2 is noisier). Sigma^(-1) = diag(1, 0.25).
      w = Sigma^(-1)(2, 2) = (2, 0.5); b = -(1/2)(2, 2).(2, 0.5) = -(1/2)(4 + 1)
      = -2.5. Boundary: 2 x_1 + 0.5 x_2 = 2.5 (it passes through the
      midpoint (1, 1): 2 + 0.5 = 2.5 OK). The weight on the noisy feature is
      four times smaller. Classify (2, 0): 4 + 0 - 2.5 = 1.5 > 0: class 1.
      VERIFIED with simulation (40,000 points per class): scikit-learn
      LinearDiscriminantAnalysis gives w = (1.987, 0.507), b = -2.494
      (theory: (2, 0.5), -2.5).
   Priors: with pi_1 = 0.8 and pi_0 = 0.2 add ln(0.8/0.2) = 1.386 to b: the
      boundary moves toward class 0, enlarging class 1's region.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: LDA weights show how to combine features to best separate
   the classes; projections onto discriminant axes are used for
   visualization and dimension reduction (supervised, unlike PCA, which
   ignores labels).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: using LDA with strongly non-normal features or unequal
   covariances without checking; p > n without shrinkage (singular
   Sigma); ignoring priors under imbalance; confusing LDA with Latent
   Dirichlet Allocation (topic model).
parts.J:
RELATED: logistic regression has the SAME linear form of the log-odds.
   Difference: LDA models the joint distribution of x and class (a
   generative classifier); it is more statistically efficient when the
   Gaussian assumptions hold, while logistic regression makes no
   distributional assumption on x (discriminative) and is more robust
   when they fail. PCA vs LDA: PCA maximizes variance (unsupervised);
   LDA maximizes class separation (supervised).

D. CONCEPT: the boundary is placed between the class means, adjusted for the
   shape of the (common) covariance: directions where the data are very
   spread contribute less; the priors shift the boundary toward the less
   likely class. Whitening (multiplying by Sigma^(-1/2)) turns the problem
   into "nearest class mean" in a spherical space.

   quadratic curves, more parameters, needs more data.

   - ln N(x; mu_0, Sigma). The Gaussian log-density is -(1/2)(x - mu)^T Sigma^(-1)
   (x - mu) + constant; expanding the quadratic form, the term x^T Sigma^(-1) x
   is the same for both classes and cancels, leaving a LINEAR function
   of x. Setting it to zero gives w and b above.
G. WORKED EXAMPLES
   Simple: mu_0 = (0, 0), mu_1 = (2, 2), Sigma = I (identity), equal priors:
      w = mu_1 - mu_0 = (2, 2); b = -(1/2)(2, 2).(2, 2) = -4: boundary 2 x_1 + 2 x_2
      = 4, i.e. x_1 + x_2 = 2: the perpendicular bisector of the segment
      joining the means.
   Moderate: Sigma = diag(1, 4) (feature 2 is noisier). Sigma^(-1) = diag(1, 0.25).
      w = Sigma^(-1)(2, 2) = (2, 0.5); b = -(1/2)(2, 2).(2, 0.5) = -(1/2)(4 + 1)
      = -2.5. Boundary: 2 x_1 + 0.5 x_2 = 2.5 (it passes through the
      midpoint (1, 1): 2 + 0.5 = 2.5 OK). The weight on the noisy feature is
      four times smaller. Classify (2, 0): 4 + 0 - 2.5 = 1.5 > 0: class 1.
      VERIFIED with simulation (40,000 points per class): scikit-learn
      LinearDiscriminantAnalysis gives w = (1.987, 0.507), b = -2.494
      (theory: (2, 0.5), -2.5).

      boundary moves toward class 0, enlarging class 1's region.

   the classes; projections onto discriminant axes are used for
   visualization and dimension reduction (supervised, unlike PCA, which
   ignores labels).
I. MISTAKES: using LDA with strongly non-normal features or unequal
   covariances without checking; p > n without shrinkage (singular
   Sigma); ignoring priors under imbalance; confusing LDA with Latent
   Dirichlet Allocation (topic model).
J. RELATED: logistic regression has the SAME linear form of the log-odds.
   Difference: LDA models the joint distribution of x and class (a
   generative classifier); it is more statistically efficient when the
   Gaussian assumptions hold, while logistic regression makes no
   distributional assumption on x (discriminative) and is more robust
   when they fail. PCA vs LDA: PCA maximizes variance (unsupervised);
   LDA maximizes class separation (supervised).

F48.3  LINEAR DISCRIMINANT ANALYSIS
A. NAME: Linear discriminant analysis (Fisher/Gaussian discriminant).

     Assumptions: within each class k the features are multivariate normal
        x | class k ~ N(mu_k, Sigma)  with the SAME covariance Sigma for all
        classes; prior class probabilities pi_k.

     LINEAR DISCRIMINANT FUNCTION for class k:
        delta_k(x) = x^T Sigma^(-1) mu_k - (1/2) mu_k^T Sigma^(-1) mu_k + ln pi_k
     Classify to argmax_k delta_k(x).

sections.title: FEATURE SELECTION AND INTERACTIONS BETWEEN FEATURES

blocks.rawText:
WHY SELECT FEATURES: reduce overfitting and variance (Module 46), improve
interpretability, speed, and robustness; remove noise and redundant
(collinear) variables. Irrelevant features especially harm distance-based
methods (k-NN, RBF kernels: distances are dominated by noise) and
flexible models with small n. With p >> n any model can fit noise
(Module 46.6: leakage example).
THREE FAMILIES
   FILTER: score each feature independently of the model (correlation,
      ANOVA F-statistic, chi-square, mutual information) and keep the top
      ones. Fast, but blind to interactions and redundancy.
   WRAPPER: search over subsets using the model's CV performance: forward
      selection (add the best feature), backward elimination, recursive
      feature elimination (RFE). Accounts for interactions; costly and
      prone to selection bias (nested CV needed).
   EMBEDDED: selection happens during fitting: lasso (L1 penalty sets
      coefficients exactly to 0), elastic net, tree/forest importances,
      L1-regularized logistic regression.
VERIFIED EXAMPLE (lasso): n = 100 observations, 50 standard-normal features,
   only features 0-4 truly matter (coefficients 3, -2, 1.5, 1, -1), noise sd 1.
   LassoCV (5-fold) selects features 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and one spurious feature
   (index 17, tiny coefficient -0.03): estimated coefficients 2.89, -1.87,
   1.22, 0.85, -0.91 (shrunk toward 0 relative to the truth, the price of
   regularization).
RULES: do selection INSIDE the cross-validation loop (a Pipeline); do not
   select using the test data; check stability across resamples; combine
   with domain knowledge; correlated features may be selected
   arbitrarily (lasso picks one of a correlated group); selection is
   not causal discovery.

blocks.title: INTERACTIONS BETWEEN FEATURES
blocks.formulaBody:
AND FORMULA: x_1 and x_2 INTERACT if the effect of x_1 on the outcome
   depends on the value of x_2. Linear model with an interaction term:
        f(x) = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_3 x_1 x_2.
   The effect (slope) of x_1 is  b_1 + b_3 x_2.

parts.B:
DEFINITION AND FORMULA: x_1 and x_2 INTERACT if the effect of x_1 on the outcome
   depends on the value of x_2. Linear model with an interaction term:
        f(x) = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_3 x_1 x_2.
   The effect (slope) of x_1 is  b_1 + b_3 x_2.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: b_3 the interaction coefficient (b_3 = 0 means no interaction:
   effects are additive).
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: b = (1, 2, 3, -1.5): slope of x_1 is 2 at x_2 = 0, 0.5 at x_2 = 1 and
   -1 at x_2 = 2: the effect of x_1 even CHANGES SIGN as x_2 grows (an
   advertisement works for young customers but hurts for old ones).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: additive models (linear, logistic) cannot represent
   interactions unless product terms are added; trees capture them
   naturally (a split on x_2 within a branch of x_1); kernels and neural
   networks learn them implicitly. XOR is the extreme case with NO main
   effects at all.
parts.E:
CAUTIONS: main effects alone may mislead when an interaction exists;
   include main effects when including their product; interaction terms
   increase collinearity (center variables first, Module 40.6) and the
   number of parameters (p(p-1)/2 pairs).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: interactions change the effect of a variable across
   groups (effect modification).
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: interpreting main effects alone when an interaction
   is present; omitting the main effects.
parts.J:
RELATED: polynomial features, feature crosses, partial dependence plots,
   SHAP interaction values.

sections.title: KERNEL METHODS AND THE RBF KERNEL

blocks.title: KERNEL FUNCTIONS AND THE KERNEL TRICK
blocks.formulaBody:
a KERNEL K(x, z) computes an inner product in a (possibly very
   high-dimensional) feature space without constructing it:
        K(x, z) = phi(x) . phi(z).
   Common kernels:
     Linear:         K(x, z) = x^T z
     Polynomial:     K(x, z) = (gamma x^T z + r)^d
     RBF (Gaussian): K(x, z) = exp( -gamma |x - z|^2 ),  gamma = 1/(2 sigma^2)
   VALIDITY (Mercer): K must be symmetric and positive semi-definite: for any
   points, the Gram matrix [K(x_i, x_j)] is a PSD matrix (F9.5).

parts.B:
FORMULA: a KERNEL K(x, z) computes an inner product in a (possibly very
   high-dimensional) feature space without constructing it:
        K(x, z) = phi(x) . phi(z).
   Common kernels:
     Linear:         K(x, z) = x^T z
     Polynomial:     K(x, z) = (gamma x^T z + r)^d
     RBF (Gaussian): K(x, z) = exp( -gamma |x - z|^2 ),  gamma = 1/(2 sigma^2)
   VALIDITY (Mercer): K must be symmetric and positive semi-definite: for any
   points, the Gram matrix [K(x_i, x_j)] is a PSD matrix (F9.5).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: phi(x) a feature map (possibly infinite-dimensional); gamma > 0
   (bandwidth parameter), sigma the length scale; d degree; |x - z|^2
   squared Euclidean distance.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: many algorithms (SVM, ridge regression, PCA) use data only through
   inner products x_i^T x_j. Replace them by K(x_i, x_j) and the same
   algorithm draws a linear boundary in the feature space phi(x), which is
   a NONLINEAR boundary in the original space. Because only K is needed,
   huge or infinite feature spaces cost nothing extra.
   The RBF kernel is a SIMILARITY measure: 1 for identical points, near 0 for
   far-apart points; each training point contributes a "bump" of width
   sigma.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   (1) Polynomial of degree 2 is an inner product in an explicit space:
       K(x, z) = (x^T z)^2 = phi(x).phi(z) with phi(x) = (x_1^2, sqrt2 x_1 x_2, x_2^2).
       Check x = (1, 2), z = (3, 1): x^T z = 5, K = 25. phi(x) = (1, 2.828, 4),
       phi(z) = (9, 4.243, 1): dot = 9 + 12 + 4 = 25. Same number, without
       computing phi.
   (2) RBF values with gamma = 0.5, x = (0, 0): z = (0, 0): K = 1; z = (1, 1):
       K = exp(-0.5 * 2) = 0.368; z = (2, 0): K = exp(-0.5 * 4) = 0.135.
   (3) Effect of gamma (verified, C = 1, 400 noisy points, RBF SVM; train/test
       accuracy and support-vector count):
          gamma = 0.01: 0.880 / 0.810 (138 SVs): too smooth (nearly linear)
          gamma = 0.1 : 0.885 / 0.840 (94)
          gamma = 1   : 0.895 / 0.855 (66)  <- best test accuracy
          gamma = 10  : 0.925 / 0.845 (92)
          gamma = 100 : 0.970 / 0.795 (169): overfit
          gamma = 1000: 1.000 / 0.625 (200): memorizes every point; every
                        training point is a support vector.
       Small gamma = wide bumps = smooth, high bias; large gamma = narrow
       bumps = wiggly, high variance (overfitting). Tune gamma jointly with
       C (Module 47) on a log scale; standardize features first.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: gamma controls the radius of influence of a single
   training example. The RBF kernel's implied feature space is infinite
   dimensional, yet fits with n points are determined by the n x n Gram
   matrix: cost grows with n (n^2 memory), which limits kernel methods to
   moderate n (tens of thousands).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: not scaling features (distances dominated by the largest
   scale); gamma too large; assuming a kernel is always better than a
   linear model (with p >> n a linear kernel is usually enough); using
   an invalid (non-PSD) similarity as a kernel.
parts.J:
RELATED: kernel ridge regression, Gaussian processes, kernel PCA;
   random Fourier features for large-scale approximation.

       K(x, z) = (x^T z)^2 = phi(x).phi(z) with phi(x) = (x_1^2, sqrt2 x_1 x_2, x_2^2).
       Check x = (1, 2), z = (3, 1): x^T z = 5, K = 25. phi(x) = (1, 2.828, 4),
       phi(z) = (9, 4.243, 1): dot = 9 + 12 + 4 = 25. Same number, without
       computing phi.
   (2) RBF values with gamma = 0.5, x = (0, 0): z = (0, 0): K = 1; z = (1, 1):
       K = exp(-0.5 * 2) = 0.368; z = (2, 0): K = exp(-0.5 * 4) = 0.135.
   (3) Effect of gamma (verified, C = 1, 400 noisy points, RBF SVM; train/test
       accuracy and support-vector count):
          gamma = 0.01: 0.880 / 0.810 (138 SVs): too smooth (nearly linear)
          gamma = 0.1 : 0.885 / 0.840 (94)
          gamma = 1   : 0.895 / 0.855 (66)  <- best test accuracy
          gamma = 10  : 0.925 / 0.845 (92)
          gamma = 100 : 0.970 / 0.795 (169): overfit
          gamma = 1000: 1.000 / 0.625 (200): memorizes every point; every
                        training point is a support vector.
       Small gamma = wide bumps = smooth, high bias; large gamma = narrow
       bumps = wiggly, high variance (overfitting). Tune gamma jointly with
       C (Module 47) on a log scale; standardize features first.
H. INTERPRETATION: gamma controls the radius of influence of a single
   training example. The RBF kernel's implied feature space is infinite
   dimensional, yet fits with n points are determined by the n x n Gram
   matrix: cost grows with n (n^2 memory), which limits kernel methods to
   moderate n (tens of thousands).
I. MISTAKES: not scaling features (distances dominated by the largest
   scale); gamma too large; assuming a kernel is always better than a
   linear model (with p >> n a linear kernel is usually enough); using
   an invalid (non-PSD) similarity as a kernel.
J. RELATED: kernel ridge regression, Gaussian processes, kernel PCA;
   random Fourier features for large-scale approximation.

      perpendicular to the segment joining them, through its midpoint:
      x_1 + x_2 = 1, i.e. w = (1, 1), b = -1. Margin = 2/|w| = 2/sqrt 2 = 1.414

      (linear SVC, very large C): w = (1, 1), b = -1, margin 1.414, support
      vectors (0, 0) and (1, 1); the other two points do not matter (move
      them away from the boundary and nothing changes).

   the model is stable with respect to the other points.

   (F11.4).

blocks.title: SOFT-MARGIN SVM, THE PARAMETER C AND REGULARIZATION
blocks.formulaBody:
minimize (1/2)|w|^2 + C sum_i xi_i
       subject to  y_i (w^T x_i + b) >= 1 - xi_i,  xi_i >= 0.
     Equivalent unconstrained form:
       minimize (1/2)|w|^2 + C sum_i max(0, 1 - y_i f(x_i))
     i.e. L2 REGULARIZATION on w plus the HINGE LOSS h(m) = max(0, 1 - m),
     m = y f(x) the margin of a point.

parts.A: NAME: Soft-margin SVM (hinge loss plus L2 regularization).
parts.B:
FORMULA
     minimize (1/2)|w|^2 + C sum_i xi_i
       subject to  y_i (w^T x_i + b) >= 1 - xi_i,  xi_i >= 0.
     Equivalent unconstrained form:
       minimize (1/2)|w|^2 + C sum_i max(0, 1 - y_i f(x_i))
     i.e. L2 REGULARIZATION on w plus the HINGE LOSS h(m) = max(0, 1 - m),
     m = y f(x) the margin of a point.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: xi_i >= 0 slack: how far point i violates the margin (xi_i = 0:
   correct and outside the margin; 0 < xi_i < 1: inside the margin but
   correct; xi_i > 1: misclassified); C > 0 the penalty weight on
   violations (C = 1/lambda).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: real data overlap, so allow margin violations but pay for them.
   C balances two goals: a wide margin (small |w|: simple, smooth) versus
   few violations (low training error). Regularization = the penalty on
   |w|^2.
   C LARGE: violations are expensive: narrow margin, fits the training data
      closely: LOW BIAS, HIGH VARIANCE (overfit risk).
   C SMALL: violations cheap: wide margin, simple boundary: HIGH BIAS, LOW
      VARIANCE (underfit risk).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: standardize features; choose C (and kernel parameters) by
   cross-validation on a log grid (Module 47); training cost grows between
   O(n^2) and O(n^3), so SVMs suit small/medium data (use linear SVM /
   SGD for very large n). Outputs are scores, not probabilities (Platt
   scaling adds them).
parts.G:
VERIFIED EXPERIMENT (linear SVM; 400 points with 10% label noise; train/test
   accuracy, number of support vectors, margin width 2/|w|):
        C         train   test    SVs    margin
        0.001     0.505   0.505   198    13.10   (w almost 0: underfit)
        0.01      0.860   0.805   156     2.99
        0.1       0.875   0.825   106     1.43
        1         0.885   0.855    87     1.04
        100       0.880   0.860    84     0.97
        10000     0.880   0.860    84     0.97   (no further change)
   As C grows the margin narrows (13.1 down to 0.97), fewer points are
   inside it (SVs drop from 198 to 84), and training accuracy rises. Test
   accuracy rises and then plateaus (the data are nearly linearly
   separable apart from noise).
   LOGISTIC REGRESSION with L2 penalty (scikit-learn C = 1/lambda, inverse strength):
        C         train   test    |w|
        0.001     0.870   0.810   0.073
        0.01      0.855   0.795   0.449
        0.1       0.880   0.810   1.179
        1         0.875   0.820   1.831
        100       0.885   0.825   2.070
   Strong regularization (small C) shrinks the weights |w| toward 0 (and
   the predicted probabilities toward the prior); weak regularization lets
   |w| grow (and, for separable data, diverge).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: SVM, ridge, logistic regression with a penalty, and weight
   decay in neural networks are all REGULARIZED EMPIRICAL RISK MINIMIZATION:
        minimize  (1/n) sum_i L(y_i, f(x_i)) + lambda * (complexity of f),
   differing in the loss L (hinge, logistic, squared) and the penalty (L2,
   L1).
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: unscaled features; confusing C (penalty on errors: large
   C = weak regularization) with lambda (large lambda = strong
   regularization): C and lambda are inverses; scikit-learn's C for
   LogisticRegression/SVC is the INVERSE of regularization strength;
   tuning on the test set; using accuracy on imbalanced data (use
   class_weight and suitable metrics).
parts.J: RELATED: ridge/lasso (Modules 40, 47), early stopping, dropout.

blocks.title: COMPARISON TABLE: LOSS FUNCTIONS FOR CLASSIFICATION (margin m = y f(x), y = +/-1)
blocks.rawText:
Loss             Formula                    Convex?  Used by
  0-1 loss         1[m <= 0]                  no       evaluation (error rate)
  Hinge            max(0, 1 - m)              yes      SVM
  Logistic         ln(1 + e^(-m))             yes      logistic regression
  Squared          (1 - m)^2                  yes      least squares classifier / LDA
  Exponential      e^(-m)                     yes      AdaBoost
  The 0-1 loss is not differentiable and non-convex, so training uses smooth
  convex SURROGATES (Module 43); all penalize margins m < 1, but the
  logistic loss never becomes exactly zero (it keeps pushing the weights
  larger on separable data) while the hinge loss is exactly zero beyond the
  margin (sparse in support vectors).

   LOGISTIC REGRESSION with L2 penalty (scikit-learn C = 1/lambda, inverse strength):
        C         train   test    |w|
        0.001     0.870   0.810   0.073
        0.01      0.855   0.795   0.449
        0.1       0.880   0.810   1.179
        1         0.875   0.820   1.831
        100       0.885   0.825   2.070
   Strong regularization (small C) shrinks the weights |w| toward 0 (and
   the predicted probabilities toward the prior); weak regularization lets
   |w| grow (and, for separable data, diverge).
H. INTERPRETATION: SVM, ridge, logistic regression with a penalty, and weight
   decay in neural networks are all REGULARIZED EMPIRICAL RISK MINIMIZATION:
        minimize  (1/n) sum_i L(y_i, f(x_i)) + lambda * (complexity of f),
   differing in the loss L (hinge, logistic, squared) and the penalty (L2,
   L1).
I. COMMON MISTAKES: unscaled features; confusing C (penalty on errors: large
   C = weak regularization) with lambda (large lambda = strong
   regularization): C and lambda are inverses; scikit-learn's C for
   LogisticRegression/SVC is the INVERSE of regularization strength;
   tuning on the test set; using accuracy on imbalanced data (use
   class_weight and suitable metrics).
J. RELATED: ridge/lasso (Modules 40, 47), early stopping, dropout.

COMPARISON TABLE: LOSS FUNCTIONS FOR CLASSIFICATION (margin m = y f(x), y = +/-1)
  Loss             Formula                    Convex?  Used by
  0-1 loss         1[m <= 0]                  no       evaluation (error rate)
  Hinge            max(0, 1 - m)              yes      SVM
  Logistic         ln(1 + e^(-m))             yes      logistic regression
  Squared          (1 - m)^2                  yes      least squares classifier / LDA
  Exponential      e^(-m)                     yes      AdaBoost
  The 0-1 loss is not differentiable and non-convex, so training uses smooth
  convex SURROGATES (Module 43); all penalize margins m < 1, but the
  logistic loss never becomes exactly zero (it keeps pushing the weights
  larger on separable data) while the hinge loss is exactly zero beyond the
  margin (sparse in support vectors).

COMPARISON TABLE: MAIN CLASSIFIERS AT A GLANCE
  Model                Boundary             Key assumption/idea             Hyperparameters
  Logistic regression  linear               log-odds linear in x            C (L2/L1 strength)
  LDA                  linear               Gaussian classes, equal Sigma   shrinkage, priors
  QDA                  quadratic            Gaussian classes, own Sigma_k   regularization
  Linear SVM           linear               maximum margin                  C
  RBF-kernel SVM       smooth nonlinear     similarity to support vectors   C, gamma
  Decision tree        axis-parallel boxes  recursive purity gain           depth, leaf size, ccp
  Random forest        smoother boxes       averaged decorrelated trees     n_trees, max_feat
  k-NN                 local, irregular     similar x have similar y        k, metric, scaling
  Neural network       very flexible        learned features                architecture, lr
DATA SCIENCE LINK: a standard workflow: (1) baseline (majority class), (2)
regularized logistic regression, (3) tree ensemble, (4) possibly RBF SVM or
a neural network, comparing with nested/repeated CV on metrics suited to
the costs (Module 46), tuning with random search (Module 47), and
inspecting decision boundaries and errors to understand what each family
can represent.
